docs.title: Building apps for the Cardputer Zero
docs.text: An independent guide for building many kinds of applications on the CardputerZero Linux handheld: utilities, notes, games, networking tools, media and peripheral apps. Start with official foundations, choose only the facilities your app needs, and preserve useful lessons from real projects.

docs.title: Scope and starting point
docs.text:
This guide targets the CardputerZero's Debian arm64/APPLaunch environment. The original ESP32 Cardputer and Cardputer ADV need different firmware, input and packaging instructions. Hardware/image variants can differ; document your tested profile and probe capabilities instead of assuming every device has a camera or Cap.

No radio, Python backend, local socket or background service is required by the guide. C++/LVGL with the official Template is the main native UI recipe. Other languages/toolkits can follow the same launcher, keyboard, privacy and package contracts with their own rendering/build implementations.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
New to this device? Build your first app in the desktop simulator. You don't need a Cardputer Zero for this first build. Start with the short route if you want to see what to read and what to skip.

Open the counter with 8, try C/Right and Z/Left, then press Esc to go back. Once it works, change the greeting and add your own reset action. Simulator capture: official Template, M5Stack CardputerZero Community (MIT); annotations added.

Ready to use a handheld? The optional first device app walks through installing, updating and removing a two-page saved counter. If a build runs on your desktop but not on the device, start with the symptom-first troubleshooting page.

Returning with a specific task? Use the project selector. Use the chapters below as a reference. Library decisions and historical Mesh lessons are separate resources further down this page.

docs.text:

For deeper background, read 1, 2 and 3. Then choose the UI/build path and project sections that apply. Chapter numbers and paths are retained for existing links; 7. LoRa bring-up is optional.

docs.title: Optional project sections
docs.text: The project selector covers local utilities, persistent text/messaging, GPS/maps, camera/QR, NFC/other hardware, networked apps and audio/media. Each section distinguishes transferable patterns, actual examples and qualification still required for a new app. A radio antenna rule does not become a calculator requirement; a camera example does not certify every image's camera stack.

docs.title: Official foundations and focused contributions
docs.text:
Use the component comparison to see what the official Template, launcher/shared SDK and AppBuilder already provide, where my Mesh code is specific to that app, and which gaps are worth addressing upstream.

The first prepared keyboard contribution adds the official symbol map, full text input, an optional editor example and raw-event/editor tests to a pinned official Template. It is a reviewable proposal, not an accepted upstream release or a new general framework.

docs.title: Personal reusable library
docs.text:
The UI preference record tracks my design decisions: the exact Mesh home carousel and Mesh list-selection base are confirmed; submenu chevrons and overflow indicators are specified. Other components remain open.

The carousel position indicator is the first small LVGL component for the shared home-menu pattern.

My library principles record the preferences and design choices I want to reuse across my apps, including appearance, interaction, application logic and backend organization. They complement official foundations and distinguish personal choices, useful alternatives and demonstrated improvements. I review each meaningful departure before deciding what to keep or share. These choices remain separate from the general guide's platform requirements.

The source inventory and proposed version 0.1 scope compare Mesh, Surveyor and NFC Tools, with file hashes, extraction candidates, open preferences and licensing/qualification boundaries. The official keyboard/input evaluation records the first use/adapt decision: official shared input for that runtime, with a focused Template extension considered separately. The official UI/shell evaluation records the next decision: reuse official foundations and adapt presentation to my preferences, preserving lifecycle, input and backend ownership.

docs.text: The prepared report and review package explain the improvements, exact sources, tests, licenses and remaining checks, including Mesh's deliberate modular UI/supervisor design. The package is prepared for review; no upstream PR, Store submission or new general library is implied.

docs.title: Worked examples and preserved learning
docs.text:
The first counter walkthrough is the small starting example. The independent-reader check records how to test the guide without the original chat context; that check is still pending.

Mesh contributed many lessons, but it is one application. The Mesh case study retains detailed state, privacy, conversation, camera and licensing examples with pinned implementation/evidence. The lesson index explains where those lessons now live. The earlier guide remains available through its linked Git revision.

Keep source-level tests, container checks, actual-device qualification and Store admission separate. No test count guarantees security, hardware compatibility or approval for a different application.

docs.title: Release and contribution checks
docs.text:
Use the Store readiness checklist and offline preflight tool to inspect a listing and its actual installer without authentication, upload or submission. Official policy/catalog revisions are pinned and reviewed; a passing local report is not a Store acceptance.

Corrections, focused examples and tested improvements are welcome. Prefer reusing or contributing to official components. Consider a separate library only after recurring needs or shared preferences, two unrelated consumers and a maintenance/compatibility plan justify it.

docs.title: 1. The platform
docs.text: Before you write a line of code, know what you're building on — it shapes every later decision.

docs.title: The device
docs.text:
The CardputerZero is a card-sized handheld built on the Raspberry Pi CM0 (quad-core Cortex-A53 at 1 GHz, 512 MB RAM), with a 1.9" 320×170 LCD, a 46-key keyboard, a battery, Wi-Fi, a camera, and expansion for M5Stack's "Cap" add-ons (including a LoRa SX1262 radio). Storage is microSD.

Three facts dominate app design:

  • The screen is a fixed 320×170. Tiny and wide. Nothing reflows; you design every screen for exactly these pixels.
  • Input is keyboard-only. No touch, no mouse. All navigation is keys (see the keyboard chapter).
  • RAM is tight (~350 MB usable) and the stock image swaps even at idle, because a full desktop stack runs hidden behind the launcher. Keep your resident set and your buffers small.

docs.title: Supported profiles
docs.text: This chapter describes the original CardputerZero Linux profile used by the worked example. State the actual board/image, RAM and available peripherals for your app; Lite/other revisions may omit sensors or use different resources. Measure memory/startup on that supported profile rather than treating one image's idle memory use as a permanent property of every device. ESP32 Cardputer/ADV firmware and packaging are outside this guide's Linux target.

docs.title: The operating system
docs.text:
It runs Debian (Trixie) on arm64 — in practice a Raspberry Pi OS base, built with M5Stack's fork of pi-gen. That means the familiar Debian/Raspberry-Pi toolbox is all there: apt, systemd, Python 3, SSH, /sys and /dev, the gpio/spi/i2c groups. If you've shipped software for a Raspberry Pi, most of your instincts transfer.

Because a complete desktop stack (display manager, panel, file manager, and friends) runs behind the launcher, some RAM and CPU are already spoken for. Budget accordingly.

docs.title: The launcher: APPLaunch
docs.text:
The home screen is APPLaunch, an LVGL 9.5 app that runs as a systemd user service. It scans installed apps, shows them in a grid, and launches the one you pick. Two things matter for you as a developer:

  • APPLaunch is the entry point for your app. You don't write your own boot/menu; you register with APPLaunch (via files your package installs) and it runs you. The contract for that is in how an app lives on the device.
  • It hands your app the framebuffer and the keyboard directly. A graphical app has no text console — APPLaunch opens the display and the shared keyboard input device and passes them to your process. Your app draws to the framebuffer and reads the same keyboard everything else does.

The launcher grabs the keyboard and shares it with the running app (it does not take exclusive ownership), so your app reads the same evdev device the launcher does.

docs.title: The Store
docs.text:
There's a first-party Store app for installing community apps. Under the hood it is not an apt source — it reads a catalog (a JSON registry hosted on GitHub Pages), downloads the chosen app's .deb from a GitHub repository, and installs that local file with apt. Dependencies resolve from the normal Debian/Raspberry-Pi archives.

The practical consequences for you:

  • Everything is a normal .deb. There is no proprietary app format. If you can build a well-formed Debian package, you can ship an app — through the Store, or just as a GitHub release people install by hand.
  • The Store never runs apt-get update. It installs your .deb against whatever package lists are already on the device. So any dependency you declare must already be installable from the base archives, be legally/operationally maintainable as an app-private bundle, or be an explicitly documented external prerequisite with runtime compatibility checks. Choose and test the dependency plan on a fresh supported image; a description alone does not install a dependency.

Publishing to the Store is optional — you can distribute entirely through your own GitHub releases. But even if you do, matching the Store's conventions (honest metadata, a real icon, 320×170 screenshots, no root) is what makes an app look trustworthy.

docs.title: What "good" means here
docs.text:
Throughout this guide, a good app is one that:

  • reads cleanly at 320×170 and is fully usable from the keyboard,
  • feels native — it looks like it belongs next to the built-in apps,
  • runs unprivileged (or escalates narrowly and honestly),
  • is open, reproducible, and ships its licenses and attributions,
  • and never pretends to do less than it does.

The rest of this guide is how to get there. Start with how an app lives on the device.

docs.title: 2. How an app lives on the device
docs.text: An app on the CardputerZero is a Debian package. There is no special "app format" — the launcher just reads standard files that your .deb drops in known places. So the whole job of "shipping an app" is: build a well-formed .deb that contains the right pieces. This chapter is what those pieces are, learned by taking the device's own apps apart (they're the reference for doing it right).

docs.title: An app is a .deb
docs.text: Every app — the built-in ones and the Store ones — is a .deb installed with apt/dpkg. Store apps are the same kind of package; they just additionally carry catalog metadata (app-builder.json). So everything below is simply "what a good package contains."

docs.title: Where the pieces go
docs.text:
A typical app installs this layout:

Path Purpose /usr/bin/<pkg> or /usr/share/APPLaunch/bin/<pkg> the executable or a launcher wrapper; use package-related names /usr/share/APPLaunch/applications/<app>.desktop the launcher entry (how it appears and starts) /usr/share/APPLaunch/share/images/<app>.png the icon, referenced from the .desktop relative to /usr/share/APPLaunch/ /usr/share/<App>/… app data/assets (fonts, sounds, images) — not next to the binary /usr/share/doc/<pkg>/LICENSE, THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md license and attributions, shipped inside the package

This table describes the launcher layout, not a complete Store allowlist. Check the current package acceptance rules. Existing built-in apps are behavioral references; they are not exemptions for third-party packages. In particular, the reviewed Store path policy does not generally allow /etc/sudoers.d/ or /usr/lib/systemd/user/.

Conventions worth copying: a descriptively named binary; the icon as a PNG under share/images/; bulky assets under /usr/share/<App>/; docs (license + notices) under /usr/share/doc/<pkg>/.

docs.title: The .desktop entry
docs.text:
This is the launcher contract — minimal and strict. For a graphical, unprivileged app:

[Desktop Entry]
Name=My App
Exec=/usr/share/APPLaunch/bin/My-App
Icon=share/images/my-app.png
Terminal=false
Type=Application

Key points:

  • Terminal=false is load-bearing. It tells APPLaunch this is a framebuffer app and to hand it the display and keyboard directly (via environment variables the launcher sets) — there is no text console. A graphical app that sets Terminal=true will not get a usable surface.
  • Icon is relative to /usr/share/APPLaunch/.
  • No Categories line on the device — categories live in the Store catalog, not in the on-device .desktop.

docs.title: What the launcher validates
docs.text: APPLaunch scans /usr/share/APPLaunch/applications/*.desktop and rejects an entry that is missing Name or Exec, has an invalid Icon, duplicates another app's Exec (first one wins), shadows a built-in app, or uses an "unsafe" Exec (it checks the command against a safety policy, so you can't point it at an arbitrary shell command). Design to that contract: a valid Name, Exec, and Icon, a unique Exec, and don't try to override a built-in.

docs.title: The privilege model
docs.text:
This is the most important thing to get right, and the thing the publish tooling actually enforces. Most apps need no root at all. The device user is already in the gpio, spi, and i2c groups, so SPI, GPIO, and I²C all work unprivileged. Escalate only for the few things that truly require it (raw sockets, monitor mode, firewall rules), and do it narrowly.

  • No root (most apps): Exec points straight at the binary. No sudoers file. Depends lists only the libraries you actually use.
  • Root, when truly needed: three things together —
  • Exec=/usr/bin/sudo -n -- <binary> in the .desktop,
  • a shipped /etc/sudoers.d/<pkg> granting passwordless sudo for that one binary only,
  • sudo in Depends.

The -n (non-interactive) means it fails fast if the rule is missing rather than hanging, and the grant is scoped to the single binary — never a blanket rule.

This explains a launcher mechanism used by existing apps, not a recommended Store submission recipe. The current path/installer policy can reject such a grant. Prefer an unprivileged UI and a narrow capability service; resolve any policy conflict openly rather than generating privileged files to bypass it.

A bundled systemd service that runs as root is rejected by the publish validator. Never ship a blanket NOPASSWD: ALL. If you need a privileged helper, prefer — in order — file capabilities (setcap cap_net_raw+eip on just the binary that needs raw sockets), then a scoped, sandboxed systemd unit started through a narrow policy, then — only where capabilities can't reach — a root-owned wrapper that re-validates every argument. The least-privilege ladder is covered in security and publishing.

docs.title: How the launcher runs your app
docs.text: APPLaunch launches the Exec, tracks whether the child keeps elevated rights, and — crucially — shares the keyboard input device with the child (no exclusive grab), so your app reads the same evdev device the launcher does. For a sudo -n app it runs non-interactively; if the sudoers rule isn't present, it fails fast.

docs.title: Reaching the hardware
docs.text:
How the device's own hardware apps behave — the patterns to reuse:

  • Acquire on enter, release on exit. On open, power the peripheral and claim its lines; on close, restore them to how you found them (including pins shared with the display bus). Leaving state clean is part of not breaking the next app.
  • Power rails and routing are controlled via /sys/class/leds/… (e.g. an ext_5v_out read the documented range; some switches use 1/0, not 255/0) plus the relevant GPIO.
  • GPIO via libgpiod on /dev/gpiochip0; SPI via /dev/spidevX.Y (the kernel handles chip-select); serial via /dev/ttyS0 (check the serial-console getty is disabled first); I²C via /dev/i2c-N. All usable unprivileged thanks to group membership.
  • Display: LVGL on the framebuffer, fixed 320×170.
  • Keyboard: read the shared evdev keyboard device the launcher hands you.
  • Audio: PipeWire runs in the user session. A root-elevated app must point at it explicitly (set XDG_RUNTIME_DIR and PULSE_SERVER=unix:$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/pulse/native) or sound won't reach the speaker.
  • Logging: log structured lines to the journal (journalctl). It's how you'll debug everything.

docs.title: Ship your licenses in the package
docs.text:
Even tiny built-in apps ship, under /usr/share/doc/<pkg>/, a LICENSE and a THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md that names each borrowed component with its source URL, exact reference commit, and full license text. This is the trust signal that tells a user your app is honest about what it's made of. Match it. The full attribution bar is in security and publishing.

Next: the one architectural decision that shapes everything else — an architecture that works.

docs.title: 3. An architecture that works
docs.text: Choose the simplest design that keeps this app responsive, testable and within its privilege and memory budget. The UI/backend split used by Mesh is one option. Start from the official component comparison before inventing a second platform layer. No app is required to depend on Python, a radio, a socket or a permanently running service.

docs.title: Choose the amount of machinery the app needs
docs.text:
App behavior Suitable starting point What to verify Calculator, timer, small local utility One normal user process with screen state and bounded callbacks Navigation, timing, close/reopen and memory use Notes, file indexing, network requests One UI process plus bounded worker jobs, or an existing compatible official service UI-thread delivery, cancellation, timeouts, safe saves and shutdown Hardware ownership that must outlive the UI, a child daemon, or a privilege boundary Separate service/supervisor with an explicit protocol Ownership, authentication, process cleanup, hardware restoration and reconnect state

A thread can keep a slow task off the UI; it does not create a privilege boundary. A process boundary helps only when its permissions, protocol and ownership are actually enforced. Do not add a background daemon to an otherwise local utility just to match a worked example.

docs.title: Why native LVGL for the UI
docs.text:
The official C++/LVGL Template is a useful starting point for native-looking apps with a desktop simulator. Its MVVM helpers and standard widgets reduce repeated UI plumbing. Other stacks are valid when they meet the launcher/input contract, fit the target image and deliver acceptable interaction, memory use and startup.

Choose a language/toolkit for the app's needs and available libraries. Measure startup, resident memory and input response on the supported device. Avoid broad claims that all Python interfaces are slow or that a toolkit name guarantees a polished interface. Build and packaging covers the native recipe and Python dependency choices; project sections identify additional work for media, hardware or networking.

docs.title: Why a separate supervisor
docs.text:
Use this option when a resource needs independent lifetime, explicit ownership, child-process containment or narrowly different privileges. The UI presents state; the owner performs validated actions and reports authoritative results. This can be C++, Python or another suitable implementation. It normally remains unprivileged.

UI (LVGL thread) -> validated request -> resource owner -> device / job / daemon
UI (LVGL thread) <- bounded result    <- resource owner

The UI can use a fake owner in desktop tests. Establish the simulator boundary before acquiring actual hardware. Keep the owner independent of screen rebuilds. Hold a lifetime ownership lock before replacing sockets or recovering resources. A stale PID file or broad process-name kill is not an ownership mechanism.

Kernel exit releases descriptors and GPIO requests, but does not restore sysfs power/mux values or necessarily kill detached descendants. If the app changes those resources, design stop/reap/restore ordering and recovery for abrupt death. A finally block cannot handle SIGKILL. A guardian or a correctly scoped service control group may be appropriate; test real subprocesses against fake hardware before making device claims. None of this requires adding a guardian to an app that owns no such resources. See hardware projects.

docs.title: Intents, not mechanism
docs.text:
If processes communicate, define named actions such as job.start {record_id} and job.cancel {request_id}. Validate action names, types, ranges, authorization and target identity at the resource owner. Never interpret a received command string as a shell command. Paths and URLs, if part of the app's purpose, need an explicit allowlist/sandbox or destination policy rather than blind interpolation.

A private Unix socket with bounded newline-delimited JSON is one implementation, not a universal requirement. Authenticate clients, limit frames/queues/work/time, correlate replies and define reconnect/error semantics. Workers must marshal results onto the UI thread; they must not retain or mutate LVGL objects after the view has gone away. See security.

docs.title: The MVVM shape of the UI
docs.text: When using the official Template, keep application state in its model/viewmodel and connect LVGL subjects to views with bindings. The screen manager owns screen switches; each screen and widget owns its observers, timers and LVGL objects. Keep those lifetimes explicit. Other UI stacks need an equivalent separation of state, presentation and resource ownership, rather than these exact C++ classes.

docs.title: Separate the device facts from the app logic
docs.text:
Keep display/input capabilities and board wiring in a small platform adapter. Resolve a supported board/image once and inject an interface that can be faked. Do not apply one Cap's GPIO/I2C/power values to every peripheral. Identify GPIO controllers by their documented labels where numbering can change. A presence probe must itself respect the peripheral's safe power sequence.

Use the official foundation when it fits. Adapt a small component for a documented gap and carry its tests/provenance with it. Require reuse in a second unrelated app and a maintenance plan before creating a general library. See the component decisions.

docs.title: Make the boundary authoritative
docs.text:
Keep committed state at its real owner. A successful button press is not proof of a completed write; reconnect snapshots must reflect confirmed results. Associate asynchronous work with a request ID and a stable target ID, not a vector index or pointer. Ignore late results after a view is dismissed, while still reporting any operation that actually committed. Define which client wins conflicting preferences.

For debounced local edits, distinguish a transport enqueue from owner acceptance. Keep the edit pending through rejection/disconnect and correlate acceptance to the submitted edit, so a late result cannot clear newer text or resurrect a deleted record. An idempotent/no-op save can still require a small acceptance reply without another disk write or full snapshot. Distinguish RAM-only acceptance from durable storage when the app offers a persistence opt-out. Keep retries bounded, surface permanent errors and preserve a bounded graceful-exit barrier. Retrying local state does not authorize replaying external actions or transmissions.

docs.title: Preserve identity and durable intent safely
docs.text:
An index or slot is a location, not an identity. Resolve stable identities again before accepting delayed work. Validate before equality/idempotence shortcuts: values such as Python True and 1 compare equal despite different types. For secret-bearing records, avoid exposing raw secrets or guessable plain hashes as identity. Use a suitable local keyed digest where that is the chosen design.

Commit related persistent changes consistently and recover interrupted writes. Coalesce repeated state, but retain durability barriers and request completion. Register callbacks with the actual event library used in production and test its parent/child subscription contract. Keep slow dependency probes outside lifecycle locks; guard shared references and distinguish cached version information from a fresh security/compatibility verdict.

Messaging delivery stages, conversation archives, retries and saved radio profiles are detailed in messaging projects and the preserved Mesh lessons.

Next: UI and polish.

docs.title: A documented modularity decision
docs.text: Mesh's architecture decision explains its native UI/Python owner choice: an existing client library, background reception after UI exit, explicit resource authority and independent tests. It also records extra resource/protocol/upgrade costs, same-user trust and hardware recovery limits. Describe the purpose, goal and verified benefits of a split in your own app; do not treat the word modular as automatic safety, reusable-library readiness or a reason every application needs a service.

docs.title: Worker construction and durable measurement jobs
docs.text:
Start a worker thread in the constructor body after all mutexes, condition variables, settings and queues have been initialized. C++ initializes members in declaration order; starting a thread in an earlier member initializer can expose later members before their construction. Stress/sanitizer passes alone do not prove that race absent. Cancellation/reset handoff needs one owner/lock, and views should receive owned data with generation/request identities.

When a batch is persisted, validate the exact collection being written and advance duplicate-suppression state only after its transaction commits. A failed write must permit the same acquisition token to be retried. Heavy report jobs should use a real read-only, consistent database snapshot and bounded inputs; opening a report reader must not run writer recovery or interrupt recording. Wireless Surveyor exercised these patterns in core, worker and UI regressions.

For a multi-field hardware setup, let the owner validate a complete draft before returning a bounded, expiring review token. Bind it to the requesting connection, request generation and original setup fingerprint, and check again immediately before writing. Reserve/cancel queued preparation too: cancelling only an already created preview permits a delayed worker to recreate it after the user leaves. Keep secrets in the owner when the UI only needs summaries. Preserve a recoverable previous configuration and stop on unconfirmed recovery. A serialized file transaction, live readback and power-loss guarantees are distinct claims; explain which failure cases your implementation actually covers.

docs.title: 4. UI and polish
docs.text:
Official foundation: input routing and LVGL remain in the Template. Deliberate UI choices: horizontal movement belongs to the carousel or a value; vertical movement belongs to lists. The home dots show position without borrowing focus, and a text-only battery value keeps the status bar readable. These are design choices for my apps, not vendor compatibility rules.

For home carousels, use the position indicator component below the menu label. Tick & Bell follows NFC Tools’ placement: the title starts at y=82 and the dots at y=138 on the 320×170 screen. Keep that breathing room even without a subtitle. Lists are vertical: use Up/Down for selection, not Left/Right. A numeric battery percentage can sit flush right in the top bar without a glyph.

Tick & Bell in the desktop simulator. The wider center dot marks the selected menu.

Make every screen predictable, readable and usable from the keyboard. Apply the patterns relevant to the chosen UI stack and app behavior.

The official UI/shell evaluation identifies the current Template and shared-runtime foundations. Adapt colors, menus and layouts while preserving the chosen shell's lifecycle, input and backend boundaries. The demo's page names, palette and bar dimensions are implementation choices; personal preferences remain separate from platform contracts.

docs.title: The constraints shape everything
docs.text:
• Fixed 320×170. Tiny and wide — design every screen for exactly this; nothing reflows. A few legible rows beat a dense grid. Don't cram.
  • Keyboard only. No touch, no mouse. Navigation is keys. See the keyboard.
  • Tight, swapping RAM. Keep assets small; don't hold big buffers.
  • LVGL 9.5 is the toolkit, drawing to the framebuffer. Design in the desktop simulator first (see building and packaging). Check fonts and bounds at 320×170, then qualify device input, performance and hardware separately.

docs.title: Use the MVVM + reactive structure
docs.text:
For apps built from the official LVGL Template, use its MVVM structure to keep screens consistent and state predictable. Other stacks should follow their own state/view conventions (see architecture choices):

  • State lives in a model/viewmodel as reactive subjects; the view binds to them with the reactive::bind_* helpers instead of being poked imperatively.
  • BaseScreen is the screen base; BaseWidgets the widget base. A screen_manager swaps the visible screen when the current-page subject changes.
  • Add a screen: add a page enum, extend the model/viewmodel with a show_<name>_page(), create a BaseScreen subclass under view/screens/, register it in screen_manager. One screen = one file; the only central edit is one switch case.
  • Add a widget: subclass BaseWidgets, implement build(), bind with reactive::bind_*.

docs.title: Consistent navigation is the biggest polish signal
docs.text:
Whatever navigation model you pick, make it identical on every screen — same keys, same positions, same back behavior. That consistency is what separates "polished" from "slop." Two proven approaches:

  • A fixed function-key lane / bottom bar — a row of labelled chips mapped to fixed keys, where each chip always shows what its key does, so the user never guesses. Reserve it for actions that are otherwise hard to reach on a 46-key board — not for Enter/Esc, which are already easy.
  • A d-pad model — map the device's arrow cluster (see the keyboard) to up/down/left/right selection, Enter to act, and Esc to go back everywhere (hold Esc to quit/home).

Reuse one well-made list screen for every list (menus, item lists), rather than a different layout per page.

docs.title: Forms, clear outcomes and persistent actions
docs.text:
A complete form can serve as its own review. Do not require another summary page by habit when it only repeats values the user has just checked. Keep the primary action, such as 1: Save, in a fixed action lane outside the scrolling fields. Show routine navigation under Help and in the user guide; reserve scarce footer space for useful screen actions. Give the space back to content when no action is needed. Keep the action label consistent with the actual destination (for example, Save channel versus Save profile).

After scanning/importing, explicitly show success and the decoded item's name before settings. A method label such as "QR/share link" and a count alone can look like a reset. Distinguish "loaded into an unsaved form" from "saved"; preserve local entries on validation errors and Back. Confirm the named saved result.

Validation and service-side preparation can run behind the Save action without becoming a mandatory visible review step. Keep ownership, stale-state checks, request correlation and cancellation before the first write. Ignore repeated activation while busy; a held key must not skip a consequential confirmation or save twice. Numeric shortcuts must remain ordinary characters inside text fields.

Reject invalid or unsupported actions with a concrete reason. For valid changes with material side effects, use a brief, specific explanation/consent when needed rather than repeating the whole form. A guide supplements clear UI; it does not replace privacy choices. Physical risks that software cannot determine reliably still need appropriate user instructions and narrowly scoped acknowledgment.

docs.title: Never block the UI thread
docs.text: Long work — talking to a radio, a network call, shelling out to a tool — must not run on the LVGL thread. A frozen screen reads as broken. Do the work on a bounded worker or in a resource-owning service when needed (architecture), and marshal results back to the UI thread using the toolkit's supported dispatch mechanism. Select the thread/process boundary for this application's actual needs.

docs.title: Show what's happening
docs.text:
• Show useful progress for long operations. A bounded, redacted log pane can suit a diagnostic tool; a short status or progress value can suit a simple task.
  • Show relevant status (connection or unread count) when it helps the task. Reuse the chosen foundation's supported status source and avoid redundant polling. Do not add a battery icon to the header by default. My personal preference keeps any useful battery percentage as text without a battery glyph; see the preference record.

When removing a status element, check its unchanged neighbors on the actual framebuffer, in both themes and after live updates. A desktop screenshot can miss partial-redraw problems. If hardware evidence shows a sibling being erased, invalidate the bounded status strip when needed rather than refreshing every screen or keeping a hidden decorative widget as a workaround.

Keep routine startup and reconnect preference synchronization quiet. Apply the saved setting and return a correlated acknowledgment without a success toast; confirm deliberate user changes when useful. Do not skip synchronization or suppress all notices to hide one distracting message. Failures must remain visible. Test first connection, reconnect, explicit changes, actual enforcement and error replies separately; validate any optional quiet flag as a boolean.

docs.title: Theme: support light and dark
docs.text:
• Keep colors in one constants file — never hardcode a color per widget.
  • Offer a light/dark toggle and make sure both are legible. At 320×170, contrast and font size matter more than cleverness. Test both themes in the simulator.
  • Use semantic color, not decorative — screens ask for meanings (warning, good-signal, "the row you're on") and the theme maps them to pixels. Use a border consistently to indicate selection, and keep its meaning and contrast clear.

Style a text editor's background, entered text, placeholder and cursor for the selected theme; setting only the screen background is insufficient. A widget can inherit colors from a global theme initialized earlier. Check an empty editor, entered text, focus and theme changes, including opening and closing overlays. This is an integration check, not evidence that the official widget is defective.

Treat meaningful secondary text differently from unavailable controls. A current setting value or delivery result must remain readable; a muted color must not make it look disabled. Check both foreground/background pairs in message bubbles and other colored surfaces. Pair freshness or status colors with text or shape, and retain approved component styling deliberately rather than changing it as a side effect of a global palette adjustment.

docs.title: Build screenshots into the app
docs.text: Bind a key to dump the active screen to a PNG with a small confirmation toast. You need 320×170 PNG screenshots for a Store listing (and your README) anyway, so have the app produce them itself — it's the most authentic way to capture the real screens. (On the device, the framebuffer can also be read directly from /dev/fb0 for the same effect.)

docs.title: Errors and empty states
docs.text:
• Show failures on screen, in plain words, not just in the log. A hardware app that can't reach its device should say so and what to check ("camera busy; close the other camera app").
  • Give empty states a line of guidance ("No notes yet — press Enter to create one"), not a blank panel.

docs.title: Accessibility and discoverability
docs.text: Label important actions in plain words and provide a keyboard route to every control, including scrolling information dialogs and dismissing overlays. Keep focus visible. Pair color with text/shape so color alone does not identify a failure, selection or privacy state. Check contrast in both themes and offer readable text sizes within the actual glyph inventory. Do not hide the only hint behind a long name or rely on a mouse/touch action on the device.

docs.title: Glyph discipline
docs.text: Decide the font/glyph inventory per screen and make sure every character you render actually exists in the font — a missing glyph renders as a tofu box and screams "unfinished." If you add icons (e.g. from a symbol font), confirm the sizes you use are compiled in.

docs.title: UI checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Consistent navigation on every screen; Esc always goes back; every action key labeled.
  • [ ] Reads cleanly at 320×170 — legible font, not crammed.
  • [ ] Both light and dark themes tested in the simulator.
  • [ ] UI never freezes — all slow work off the LVGL thread.
  • [ ] Long operations show progress; errors shown on screen in plain words; empty states guided.
  • [ ] Relevant status is visible; no unnecessary status bar or polling.
  • [ ] A real icon (not the template default) and real 320×170 screenshots.
  • [ ] No missing-glyph boxes anywhere.
  • [ ] No placeholder/TODO text anywhere in the UI or metadata.

docs.title: Privacy state and asynchronous overlays
docs.text:
For asynchronous settings, show confirmed, Pending and Unknown states. Expire pending actions after a deadline. Read back actual state when the underlying API requires it; editing a cache is not confirmation. Use stable record/request IDs and stop accepting a dismissed view's late results. A timeout can leave an outcome unknown; it does not prove the backend rolled a write back.

Remove observers and timers with their owning views. Never hold an LVGL pointer or a pointer into a reallocating vector across a worker callback or rebuild. Keep global Help/Esc ownership explicit so input cannot reach a hidden editor. Test navigation away, list reordering, repeated Return and disconnect while busy.

docs.title: First run and uncertain live data
docs.text:
Provide safe defaults, explain actual prerequisites, preserve existing data and make consequential actions deliberate. Ask only for settings relevant to the app. A local calculator may need no wizard. A hardware transmitter requires additional consent described in its project section. Show actionable failure reasons.

Measurements need valid values, a meaningful timestamp and a freshness policy. Show stale data as last known; unknown is different from zero. Coalesce updates and refresh age labels. Device GPS and camera details belong in GPS/maps and camera/QR.

docs.title: Persistence and redraws
docs.text:
Debounce text saves by a pause in typing, flush at defined navigation/close boundaries and keep rejected edits recoverable. Do not serialize local saves behind unrelated slow hardware jobs. Quiet hours need local-time and midnight semantics only if the app actually offers notifications.

Compare effective state before rebuilding object trees, while still handling request completion and genuine changes. Preserve selection by stable identity through reordering and define a consistent tie order. Prepare/index list data once instead of repeating searches for every visible row. Measure realistic workloads; a synthetic improvement is not a measured battery-life benefit.

Update selection styles and changed field values in place when layout is stable. Avoid reconstructing every row on each arrow key or subscribing to several subjects that each cause an identical initial rebuild. Preserve stable targets, scrolling and observer ownership. If a selected record disappears, require a safe explicit selection rather than silently acting on its replacement. Use small shared visual helpers where they simplify actual callers; keep each screen's confirmation, editing and resource lifetime explicit. Review cache ownership when consolidating records: retaining large previews can extend their memory lifetime. Selection helpers should not allocate unused styles on every unselected row.

Observe independent facts independently: a mode can change while connection state stays Online. Refresh age/freshness and time-based filters even when no new hardware event arrives. A presentation clock can update existing age labels and markers without rebuilding the whole screen; bind its callbacks to screen/object lifetime and test destruction as well as stale/future-time boundaries. Unknown state must remain unknown after disconnect. Poll only the device facts actually displayed. Measure operation counts separately from timing, using the same build and data before/after; qualify device performance separately from host results.

docs.title: Keep context and keyboard help readable
docs.text:
Keep the current task/record in a bounded header and reserve the footer for short keyboard hints or text entry. Truncate descriptive detail before information needed to understand the action's target. Check real font/pixel bounds with long names, selection, typing, scrolling and return navigation.

An LVGL outline can be clipped outside a tightly fitted parent. Use an inside border or sufficient parent clearance. Keep border plus padding insets stable so selection does not move text or resize the row. Verify both light and dark themes.

Group settings with nonselectable headings and give actions stable keys independent of display order. Navigate through selectable actions; give long overlays scrolling and an Escape path. Tests should find a setting by identity/label instead of a historic number of Down presses, especially for privacy or destructive operations.

Detailed examples remain in Mesh UI lessons. Next: the keyboard.

docs.title: Keep a complete setup in one place
docs.text:
When a task spans several settings, provide one shared setup flow with a local draft across field editors and validation errors. Several entry points can open the same flow; remove obsolete independent paths rather than keeping duplicate implementations. Show which values belong to one item and which affect the whole device. Imported settings can be suggestions without silently replacing active configuration or device-specific calibration. Offer a separate saved profile when that is useful, with its effect on the active session explicit.

Describe a saved setup's contract before applying it: what is saved, what stays unchanged, what is deliberately reset, and any prerequisite such as releasing a resource first. Do not imply that a profile restores every operating mode when it stores only configuration. A safe reset must still be predictable. Mesh's transmission/location defaults are a radio-specific example, not a rule that all applications must disable their hardware when switching profiles.

Use the fixed heading/action arrangement described under forms, with selection updated in place. Test long errors, UTF-8 byte limits, masked secrets, deep selection, both themes, Escape, repeated Return, late replies and destroyed screens. Preserve an imported token when returning to edit an unrelated field; closing setup should cancel the whole draft.

Separate local preparation, explicit Save, stored verification, live hardware readback and actual connectivity/delivery. Cancellation before Save changes nothing; once a write has started, explain that leaving cannot undo it. Report partial success and uncertain outcomes explicitly so users do not duplicate an operation. Mesh exercises this pattern in its unified channel setup; the pattern also applies to network, peripheral and other device configuration tools.

docs.title: Task clarity and recovery
docs.text:
For form actions and validation, use forms and clear outcomes; for setup scope and saved profiles, use complete setup. The personal preference record separately specifies my direct two-choice rows and selection menus.

Use Cancel-first confirmation for irreversible deletion when Undo is not available. Bind the action to a stable identity rather than a moving row. The prompt must name the scope: one item versus its history, draft or saved setup, and local copies versus copies elsewhere. Cancelling the prompt must not submit a destructive operation. Re-resolve the captured identity when confirming; an item that vanished must not be replaced by the next row. Test Cancel, Esc, repeated keys and new/reordered content while the prompt is open, and clear the pending action when the prompt closes.

Communication outcomes and search limits belong in the messaging recipe; readable values and non-color cues are covered under theme states.

Form section headings and explanatory rows are not actions. Skip them during keyboard navigation and wrapping; keep the selected field, its nearby section heading and the primary action understandable as the viewport moves. Use the selected toolkit's overflow-only scrollbar behavior and reserve space for its marker. Check both overflowing and fully visible lists.

Validate complete tasks as well as isolated screens: create/import, edit, cancel, save, reopen, switch a saved setup and recover from a failed operation. Host renders, headless replay on the actual device and a physical operator walkthrough answer different questions. Replay with synthetic commands and installed fonts can check the UI without opening hardware; it does not prove physical key input, framebuffer ownership, RF delivery or outdoor positioning.

docs.title: 5. The keyboard
docs.text:
Input is keyboard-only, and the 46-key keyboard has some sharp edges that will cost you debugging time if you don't know them up front. This chapter is the layout, the modifiers, and — most importantly — the keycode reality your app has to handle to accept real text.

The raw-evdev decoder below is the C++/LVGL Template path. The shared cp0 SDK already supplies a richer decoded keyboard-event contract; use one matching backend and avoid translating its decoded characters a second time. Other languages should implement/adapt the same behavior and independent fixture checks at their own input seam. They need not embed a C++ library just to follow this guide. See the component comparison and prepared Template contribution. The current official-input evaluation records reviewed sources, use/adapt decisions and the limits of the selected tests.

docs.title: The layout
docs.text:
46 keys, no dedicated arrow keys. Movement and symbols come from three modifiers:

  • Shift → uppercase (and the standard shifted punctuation).
  • Fn → the "orange" shortcuts: arrows, function keys, media, etc.
  • Sym → the "blue" symbols printed on the keys (?, !, @, #, …).

Each modifier works three ways: hold it while pressing a key; tap once to apply it to the next key only (sticky); tap twice to lock it on.

docs.title: Movement (Fn layer)
docs.text:
Keys Action Fn + F / X / Z / C Up / Down / Left / Right Fn + K / N Home / End Fn + L / M PageUp / PageDown Fn + Backspace Delete Hold Esc Back to the home screen

Function keys are Fn + 1…0 (F1–F10), Fn + O / P (F11/F12). Useful ones: Fn + H (app help), Fn + J (screenshot). So Fn + F / X / Z / C is your d-pad — that's the arrow cluster your UI navigates with.

docs.title: Use the official map, not a hand-built approximation
docs.text:
The authoritative references are:

  • M5Stack key specifications: printed legends, Fn functions and hold/one-shot/lock behavior.
  • Official launcher symbol decoder: the complete 32-symbol map, with a runtime override from /usr/share/keymaps/tca8418_keypad_m5stack_keymap.map.
  • Official Keyboard Guide input: examples of version-dependent modifier-state reporting. Check which kernel interface exists on the target image before adopting a backend.

Correction, 2026-11-16: an earlier version of this chapter said there was no published table and supplied 14 assignments. Three were wrong (92 was shown as colon, 80 as minus and 71 as slash), and 18 symbols were missing. The worked example inherited those errors. The device's installed map and the official launcher agree on all 32 assignments below. Do not reuse the old table.

Linux event code Symbol Linux event code Symbol 26 ! 27 @ 39 # 40 $ 41 % 43 ^ 51 & 52 * 53 ( 94 ) 55 ~ 69 backtick 70 _ 71 - 72 + 73 = 74 [ 75 ] 76 { 77 } 79 ; 80 : 81 apostrophe 82 double quote 83 < 85 > 86 backslash 89 vertical bar 90 , 91 . 92 / 93 ?

These are Linux event codes, not ASCII values, matrix positions or XKB codes (which use an offset). For example, Sym+N produces the symbol-layer code for slash, 92; translating 92 to : was an application error.

docs.title: A reusable input component
docs.text:
The worked example supplies a reusable C++ decoder and regression suite:

  • keyboard_decoder.h
  • keyboard_decoder.cpp
  • independent vendor fixture
  • raw-event/editor tests
  • LVGL/evdev integration

For a Template/raw-evdev app that needs this extension, keep the component and tests together after evaluating current official options. A shared-runtime app should consume its official decoded input contract instead of adding this decoder. Pin the source revision when copying or vendoring, preserve MIT/M5Stack attribution, and keep the fixture's upstream provenance. The component has no radio, filesystem or UI-object ownership; its caller supplies raw event code/value and current typing context. It returns a character or semantic control plus press/release state. The LVGL adapter owns device discovery, trusted keymap-file I/O, routing and repeat timing.

docs.title: The driver already selected the Sym layer
docs.text:
On the built-in tca8418c keyboard, look up a symbol-layer code in the official map before ordinary US key translation. Do not require a physical Sym-down flag to recognize it. The driver can emit that same selected symbol after a single tap, under lock, or after the app opens while Sym is already active. Reconstructing a second modifier state machine for already-translated symbols can apply the layer twice or discard valid symbols.

Scope this table to the identified built-in keyboard. A USB keyboard's code 26 normally means [, while the CardputerZero's selected symbol code 26 means !. Applying the vendor table globally corrupts standard keyboards. The worked example's generic profile is US-layout input; use a qualified xkbcommon backend if an application needs additional layouts or composition.

Keep Shift/Control/Alt state per input device. Preserve each key's press-time translation until its release, even if a modifier is released, the keymap changes, or the editor closes in between. Initialize/resynchronize available kernel state after opening a device or losing events; do not invent support for a modifier-state API that the installed kernel does not expose. Older images and newer vendor sources have different interfaces. No app needs to force access to shared I2C hardware merely to decode these already-selected symbol codes.

docs.title: Separate text from Fn actions
docs.text:
Fn arrow/Home/End/Delete codes are semantic controls, not printable characters. Help, Screenshot, PageUp/PageDown, Insert, F1-F12 and media/display actions must also remain non-text. Define what your app does with each one; an unbound action must be consumed safely rather than encoded as garbage in a draft. A one-line editor need not invent a PageUp or Insert action. System-wide media/display keys may also be handled by the platform; do not add duplicate shell-outs per app.

Global Help/Screenshot should remain reachable while editing. A visible Help popup owns input: Enter must not send the draft underneath it. Closing help must restore the same editor, text and cursor.

Consume shortcuts before LVGL delivers them to the focused widget. Returning true from your application's callback does not automatically prevent LVGL from sending the key onward. The worked example filters each new press/release in the indev read callback and exposes only unconsumed input to LVGL. Use the same route for simulator and device input; test that shortcut values never become text.

docs.title: Stream handling and focus timing
docs.text:
• Query the current typing context for each event, not once per frame. Enter can open an editor and a letter can follow within the same evdev batch.
  • Store active translations per device. Handle overlapping letter presses without dropping the second character or treating an older release as a newer release.
  • Choose one repeat owner (LVGL in the worked example); do not also replay Linux repeat records. Repeated Enter must never queue several sends.
  • On SYN_DROPPED, discard records until SYN_REPORT, cancel stale holds and resynchronize available modifiers. A lost Escape release is not an app exit.
  • EOF/disconnect must release stale input and leave the reader inert. Do not perform a blocking retry loop on the UI thread.

docs.title: Required regression coverage
docs.text:
Compile the production decoder on the development host too; hiding it under !USE_DESKTOP prevents simulator tests from exercising it. On Linux, the worked example additionally feeds synthetic input_event records through the real evdev reader, shortcut filter, LVGL indev and focused textarea, using a pipe. There is no /dev/input injection, RF or live user typing in that suite.

Cover every official symbol against an independent upstream fixture; ordinary letters and Shift; driver-selected symbols with held/released/locked modifiers; Fn cursor/Home/End/Delete; Help/Screenshot while editing; unbound Fn keys; key release order and rollover; same-batch focus changes; multiple device profiles; malformed/partial keymaps; event loss and disconnect. Check draft text and cursor, not only that a handler ran. Retain source/hash evidence for the fixture; never change both expected data and implementation solely to make a failing test pass. Verify the fixture is tracked in a clean checkout: templates often ignore *.map as linker output, so a deliberate exception is needed for a keymap fixture.

Automated event replay validates the software contract. A physical check can confirm a particular device/image's emitted events and ergonomics, but is not needed to rediscover an already-published mapping. Record those results separately and recheck compatibility when the kernel/keyboard firmware changes. Reading a shared evdev stream does not require stopping the launcher or grabbing the device; any diagnostic capture should be bounded and use synthetic input only.

docs.title: A nicety: let the d-pad keys navigate without Fn
docs.text:
The bare F / X / Z / C keys type letters, but outside a text field there's nothing to type — so many apps feel better if the bare F/X/Z/C keys act as the d-pad everywhere except while a text field is focused, and require Fn for the arrows only inside text entry. (Both still work: the Fn-translated KEY_UP/etc. keep functioning.) Switch on whether a text input is currently capturing. It removes the need to reach for Fn just to move around a menu.

Next: the full build-and-ship pipeline — building and packaging.

docs.title: Bound input work and clean up the owning device
docs.text:
A native input reader should budget raw read attempts across the complete continue_reading chain, including ignored records, modifiers, repeats and interruptions. A limit on decoded characters alone does not bound that work. Yield on exhaustion and retain queued/pending input for the next poll. Verify both modifier floods and ordinary typing across the boundary without loss/duplication.

Associate a pending hold action with its source input device. EOF, lost input and object teardown should cancel that owner's timer without synthesizing a short release/click. An unrelated device's release or deletion must not cancel the current owner's hold. Use the same cleanup contract for native and simulator adapters. Test two devices using the same key, owned deletion, loss/disconnect and simulated time passing after cleanup. Mesh's current component uses 128 raw read attempts per device poll; that is a scoped fairness bound, not a global timing guarantee.

docs.title: 6. Building and packaging
docs.text:
The C++/LVGL recipes below apply to the official CMake Template. Other stacks can use the same package/launcher/Store contract with their own build system. Python dependency plans are a separate path. A backend or service is optional.

From source to an installed .deb. Start a native app from the official CardputerZero/Template (MIT, LVGL 9.5, CMake, C++); it gives you the MVVM scaffold, the simulator, and the cross-build/packaging presets.

docs.title: Develop in the desktop simulator — and why
docs.text:
Build and run the UI in the desktop simulator first; qualify the installed app on the device separately. The template ships this: a desktop preset builds an SDL window that renders the real LVGL UI at the device's 320×170, using the same screens, widgets, fonts, and theme as the device build.

Why it's the right default:

  • The device loop is slow and fragile. Cross-compile → package → copy → install → relaunch is minutes per change, and the device's Wi-Fi can be flaky. The simulator is seconds, on your laptop, no network.
  • It uses the same UI code. Preview layout, themes and flow without the hardware. Display/input backends, installed fonts and runtime conditions still need device checks.

The simulator does not qualify actual radios, cameras or Caps. Put slow hardware work behind a bounded worker, a compatible OS service or a resource-owning supervisor as the app requires (see architecture). A single foreground process can use supported OS services without a new daemon. Use fake source adapters for the simulator and test the real source contract separately.

docs.title: Desktop build (example: macOS Apple Silicon)
docs.text:
brew install cmake ninja libpng jpeg fmt sdl2 freetype dpkg zlib
cmake --preset darwin-arm64                        # fetches LVGL 9.5 on first configure
cmake --build build/darwin-arm64 --config Release
./build/darwin-arm64/Release/<app>                 # opens the SDL window

Linux desktop: sudo apt install -y build-essential cmake ninja-build libpng-dev libjpeg-dev libfmt-dev libsdl2-dev libfreetype-dev zlib1g-dev, then the linux-x86-64 preset. (On Windows, use the win32-msvc/win32-mingw64 presets; deps come through vcpkg.) Preset families: linux-x86-64, darwin-arm64, darwin-x86-64, win32-msvc, win32-mingw64, each with -dbg/-rel.

Note: the template's README badge may say "SDL3", but the dependency it actually pins is SDL2 — trust the SDL2 install commands.

docs.title: Add a screen (the recipe)
docs.text:
Adding a screen is a few small, local edits — sources are globbed, so a new file is picked up with no CMake change:

  1. The screen file — src/view/screens/<name>_screen.{h,cpp}, subclassing BaseScreen, implementing build_content(lv_obj_t* content), calling init() in the constructor. Use the viewmodel's subjects, the asset manager's fonts, and the theme-binding helpers.
  2. The page id — add a value to the AppPage enum and bump the count.
  3. The viewmodel navigation — add show_<name>_page().
  4. The screen manager — add show_<name>_screen() and a case in its page switch.
  5. It's reachable: set the page and the manager reacts (you never load a screen directly from UI code). Wire a key/button to show_<name>_page() for direct access.

docs.title: Cross-build to a device .deb (C++)
docs.text:
cmake --preset cp0-cross                # cross toolchain; may fetch the device BSP/SDK on first run
cmake --build --preset cp0-cross-rel
cpack --preset cp0-cross-deb            # -> dist/<App>_<ver>_rev<n>_arm64.deb
  • Toolchain: aarch64-linux-gnu- (crossbuild-essential-arm64 on Debian; a corresponding cross-gcc via Homebrew on macOS).
  • Package on a Debian host. cpack needs dpkg, dpkg-shlibdeps, objdump, and readelf to resolve dependencies; other OSes may produce a .deb with wrong Depends.

The resulting package installs the layout from how an app lives on the device.

docs.title: Install on the device
docs.text:
For a worked first install, update, and rollback, use the Guide Counter walkthrough. If it does not appear or open, see device troubleshooting.

REMOTE_USER=<user> REMOTE_HOST=<device-ip> ./deploy.sh      # copies the .deb over SSH
# then, on the device:
sudo apt install --no-install-recommends ./<App>_<ver>_rev<n>_arm64.deb

For native device compilation, the official cp0-native preset is available, but keep build dependencies out of a release installer. Prefer a traceable package install for qualification; an ad hoc binary copy does not verify package paths, upgrade behavior or the exact artifact users will receive.

docs.title: Packaging a Python app
docs.text:
Choose and document a dependency plan before packaging. The Store installs against the device's available package lists; do not assume it refreshes them or installs an arbitrary Python environment for you. Three plans are possible:

Plan When it fits What you must verify Debian Depends Libraries available for the supported device image A fresh target image can resolve the actual version/architecture from its configured repositories App-private vendoring Dependencies you can legally redistribute and maintain Full dependency closure, native ABI compatibility, licenses/source obligations and a security-update process Explicit external prerequisite A separately managed daemon, hardware stack or environment Exact supported versions, installation instructions, runtime detection and a useful missing/incompatible-dependency screen

Combinations are normal. Mesh 0.1.19 uses Debian dependencies for standard OS components plus a private qualified radio executable and locked Python wheels, prepared offline for the user. Earlier Mesh versions used separate prerequisites. This is a distribution choice, not a Store requirement or a GPL bundling ban. See the worked example's installation instructions and licensing.

Test the chosen plan on a fresh supported image, then test missing/incompatible dependencies, an upgrade, a cold boot and uninstall. Dependency installation must not silently enable another daemon or start RF; inspect dependency autostart too. Record what is bundled, what Depends resolves and what the user installs. Never hide a network installer or pip install in a root maintainer script.

For the app-private vendoring plan, this is a useful recipe:

  1. Stage the on-device tree. Put the app and its full dependency closure under /usr/lib/<pkg>/site via pip install --no-compile --target /usr/lib/<pkg>/site .[extras], and delete pip's generated bin/ (its shebangs point at the build venv). Put assets/fonts under /usr/lib/<pkg>/…. Add the .desktop, the icon, a /usr/bin/<pkg> CLI wrapper, and /usr/share/doc/<pkg>/ (LICENSE, NOTICE, third-party notices, Debian copyright).
  2. Compile bytecode: python -m compileall -q --invalidation-mode unchecked-hash /usr/lib/<pkg>/site (files are read-only in /usr/lib; unchecked-hash skips the mtime check and speeds cold start).
  3. Launch via tiny /bin/sh wrappers, not a package shebang. The wrapper exports PYTHONPATH=/usr/lib/<pkg>/site and exec /usr/bin/python3 -s -m <module> "$@" (-s ignores the user site-dir; exporting PYTHONPATH means child processes resolve the same vendored packages). The APPLaunch wrapper runs the UI module; /usr/bin/<pkg> runs the CLI module.
  4. Declare the remaining system requirements. If the closure is entirely pure Python, the runtime dependency may be just python3. Native extensions can still need shared libraries: derive/check those dependencies too. A Python 3.13 environment may need Depends: python3 (>= 3.13), python3 (<< 3.14); match the tested interpreter/ABI instead of copying that range to every app. Use a fitting Section, Priority: optional, and the correct Architecture (arm64 or all).
  5. Build with dpkg-deb --root-owner-group -Zxz --build <stagedir> <out>. This matters: dpkg-deb --build on a populated directory emits real directory entries — some hand-rolled ar+tar packagers stream only files, producing a .deb with zero directory entries that won't install. Never hand-build the archive. (umask 022 for deterministic perms; set SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH + --clamp-mtime if you want byte-for-byte reproducibility.)
  6. Smoke-test the staged tree first: run python3 -s -m <module> --help with PYTHONPATH pointed at the stage. Cheap, and it catches a broken vendor.

docs.title: The app-builder.json manifest
docs.text:
The top-level fields identify the app/build; store supplies the catalog listing. Keep package, runtime, manifest and release versions aligned. The launcher icon inside the .deb and the Store icon may use separate files; validate both. The official online build also expects its packaging fields, including bin_name; an app with its own CMake/CI build must satisfy that build's contract separately. czdev publish takes an already-built installer and does not replace its contents.

Field Acceptance rule package_name Debian name, at least two characters, lowercase a-z0-9.+-, starts alphanumeric; match the .deb Package field version Match the built upstream/full version; record a Debian revision separately and use Debian version comparison for updates app_name Store title; unique after case folding and whitespace normalization store.summary Nonempty, at most 80 characters, no template placeholder store.categories One or two exact category names from the list below store.screenshots One to six real PNGs, each exactly 320×170; source paths relative to the app directory store.icon Square PNG, 128–512 pixels per side; 256 recommended store.license Accurate SPDX identifier/expression for what is distributed; the validator checks text, not legal compliance store.author Non-placeholder display_name; github should match the publishing account store.share_code Exactly four ASCII letters/digits, unique case-insensitively across the catalog; not a placeholder such as TEMP/TODO store.permissions Exactly the seven keys below, each a JSON boolean store.description, source_repo, locales Recommended by upstream policy; this guide additionally expects public source, clear prerequisites and accurate descriptions

Allowed categories: System Tools, Development, Hardware & IoT, Security, Radio & Comms, AI, Creative & Office, Media, Games, Emulators, Education, Lifestyle, Other. Labels such as Communication and Utilities are not accepted synonyms.

The seven permission keys are camera, microphone, imu, network, additional_hardware, background_service, external_display. They disclose capabilities to the user; they do not create an OS sandbox. Declare actual behavior, including a background process or networking needed by a supervisor.

czdev stages icons by basename and screenshots under screenshots/<basename>; avoid basename collisions. It records the authenticated GitHub uploader and merges nonempty listing updates into published metadata, preserving assigned identity such as uuid and an existing share code. Check code/title availability against the catalog immediately before submission; a local check cannot reserve either. Replace template authors, summaries, Maintainer and source URLs before release.

Policy references, reviewed 2026-11-16: official schema, metadata validator. The preflight lock records exact revisions/hashes.

docs.title: Package layout and installer acceptance
docs.text:
Inspect the actual .deb. The current Store checks more than non-root services:

Area Required check Identity Valid Package/Version/Maintainer, supported arm64 or all, no template identity; uploaded filename agrees with control metadata Launcher Entry at /usr/share/APPLaunch/applications/*.desktop; verify its Name/Exec/Icon and graphical Terminal=false on the device Executables /usr/bin/<name> must relate to the package name; an unrelated short helper name can fail Data/config Use package-related directories under /usr/share, /usr/lib, /opt, /var/lib; package-related configuration under /etc Shared directories Use the policy's explicit exceptions for APPLaunch, documentation, named completion/man/tmpfiles/udev files and system units Forbidden locations No /usr/local; no merged-usr alias paths such as /bin or /sbin; no unrelated shared-system filenames Services/privilege System unit names must relate to the package; no default/root User; DynamicUser=yes is recognized. No setuid/setgid files or device nodes udev No RUN, PROGRAM or IMPORT{program} commands that execute as root Maintainer scripts Read every script without executing it; the Store rejects dangerous textual patterns such as destructive deletion, disk writes, account/sudoers edits and downloaded shell pipelines Size Release asset limit is 2 GiB; this is not a sensible target size for the handheld

The authoritative install-path policy and PR validator define the exact floor. The reviewed path policy has an exception for system units, but not /usr/lib/systemd/user/; a legitimate user unit can therefore fail its path check. /etc/sudoers.d/ also has no general exception. Do not hide files in installer-generated state or weaken a working privilege model to evade validation. Resolve packaging design or ask maintainers about a policy gap.

An app that needs an on-demand background process can use a transient user service, created through systemd-run --user with fixed, reviewed arguments. This uses the normal user manager/cgroup without distributing a static unit or writing hidden privileged files. Preserve NoNewPrivileges, kill/restart policy, private umask and stop/recovery hooks. Serialize start/stop, avoid restarting an active service when a second UI opens, and stop the old service before upgrading. Test actual service properties, child cleanup, failed start and repeated launches on the supported systemd version. Archive acceptance alone cannot inspect this runtime configuration. Mesh's controller is an example; arbitrary intent fields must never select a unit, command, executable or service property. Do not assume static-unit specifiers expand inside transient command properties: the device probe found %t remained literal in ExecStopPost. Mesh constructs the Debian runtime path from the kernel UID instead. Verify the actual cleanup argument and outcome, not merely that the property was accepted.

These are automated admission checks, not an execution sandbox or a complete review of shell logic, .desktop behavior, dependencies, symlinks or hardware. Keep the independent security checklist.

Documentation size is determined by install rules, not by the folder name: Mesh 0.1.8 includes Markdown/images under /usr/share/doc/cardputerzero-mesh/docs and explicitly excludes generated PDFs. Check archive contents before claiming that guides do or do not increase installer size.

docs.title: The czdev tool and the Store
docs.text:
czdev (Python) scaffolds and publishes; it does not build the .deb (you build with cmake/cpack or the Python recipe, then hand it the file):

./czdev login                 # GitHub device-flow auth
./czdev new my-app            # scaffold from the template (renames project/launcher/icons)
./czdev publish --deb build/my-app_1.0.1_arm64.deb   # uploads binary/metadata and opens a PR
./czdev publish --meta-only                        # listing update for an existing app

publish is a mutation, not a dry run: it can create/use a fork, upload the binary to a release, commit listing assets/metadata and open a PR against CardputerZero/packages. On merge the Store promotes the accepted binary to its official release/index. Git contains metadata, not the .deb. Run the non-publishing preflight first; it performs no authentication, network requests, install, upload or PR creation. The reviewed CLI has no publish --dry-run option.

czdev performs local checks, including a fetched metadata policy. If that fetch fails, it can skip the metadata precheck; uniqueness is left to server-side CI. A local CLI success is not evidence that the entire Store gate passed. The submission records a SHA-256, which PR validation verifies. That checksum identifies bytes; it is not a developer signature or proof of safe behavior.

Publishing is optional; your own GitHub release is a separate distribution path. The release checklist covers the complete workflow and separates Store admission from hardware/security evidence.

Next: if your app drives the LoRa Cap — optional project sections. Otherwise skip to security and publishing.

docs.title: Validate the installed result
docs.text:
A manifest is not the package. Give the CMake project version, runtime About text, Debian control metadata and store manifest one consistent release version; test that they agree. Keep inherited internal build-target names separate from public package/display names. Install the real icon at the exact launcher path, plus all required supervisor files, licenses, user units and scoped policy helpers. Generate native library dependencies from the built ELF with dpkg-shlibdeps in a matching distro/architecture environment; hardcoding libfmt/libjpeg package names can produce a package that builds but cannot install.

Respect the actual minimum CMake version (the template currently needs 3.31), choose a writable package output directory, and inspect both dpkg-deb --info and dpkg-deb --contents. Check maintainer scripts, modes, sudoers with visudo -cf, and units with systemd-analyze verify. Test a clean install and cold boot on the target image. Ensure firewall/setup dependencies exist before any daemon opens a network listener. A service file with no enable/install path does not provide reboot persistence. Package installation should not silently start RF.

Keep personal checkout paths out of release binaries as well as source files: use compiler prefix maps and avoid embedding source asset paths in device builds. State which checks used mocks, containers, simulator, or real hardware; a prior review or successful build is not proof that the installed/rebooted app is safe.

Use an app-specific settings directory, binary, launcher entry and asset namespace. Two apps retaining template-app settings paths can accidentally share preferences. Migrate deliberately, and require explicit re-enabling of hardware auto-start. For INI saves, use a unique private temporary file per writer, sync before atomic rename, and sync the directory. Escape or reject line breaks in single-line values; test concurrent writers and malformed/overflowing numeric preferences.

Test the actual user service, not just systemd-analyze verify. In a user unit, filesystem sandboxing can imply a user namespace that maps host root to nobody; seccomp restrictions can imply NoNewPrivileges. Both can break an otherwise valid scoped sudo helper. Inspect the live process's UID map/NoNewPrivs and execute the real privileged check. Use a consistent privilege design; keep root-owned files protected by DAC when a fixed sudo check requires host credentials.

docs.title: Automate the matching package build
docs.text:
Use a native arm64 CI runner and a container matching the device's Debian release. Fetch qualified dependency commits explicitly, build and install the real package, then validate its dependency metadata, executable paths, service files, permissions, policy helpers and offline regressions. Disable networking and isolate the network namespace during firewall tests so a test cannot change the host's rules. Upload a checksummed candidate and corresponding source commit. A successful artifact job is still separate from RF, camera, GPS and physical cold-boot proof.

Use one authoritative version field and read it from each runtime/build path. For a split UI/backend app, install that metadata alongside the backend as well as deriving CMake's project/package version from it. Avoid independent fallback literals that silently drift when one component is bumped. Container outputs may be owned by root. Copy them into a runner-owned staging directory before writing checksums/source metadata and uploading the artifact. Download the finished artifact and verify both its checksum and source commit.

On upgrade, matching installed-file hashes does not prove the live process loaded them. Coordinate a restart through the resource owner's lifecycle, then check its reported version and socket peer PID against the service's MainPID. Starting an already active unit leaves its old code running. Determine how restart affects in-flight work and hardware first; do not enable a transmitter or restore privacy opt-ins merely to produce a healthy-looking status. Verify actual privilege state and preserved user settings as well as the files.

Inspect supported command-line arguments before a smoke test. Do not assume a GUI executable implements --version or --help: an ignored argument can launch the UI, claim the display/input devices or initialize hardware, especially from a root installation shell. Use About or package metadata when a version option is not documented; neither alone establishes which code an existing service has loaded. A future app can offer an explicit read-only version command that exits before UI/hardware initialization.

Use a consistent private snapshot for preservation checks. For SQLite, use its backup facility or another documented consistency method; comparing live database file bytes can misread WAL/checkpoint activity as data loss. Compare logical rows and relevant configuration fields, keeping keys and raw records out of public logs. Classify bookkeeping differences only after inspection, and distinguish upgrade effects from edits the operator makes during a walkthrough. Do not restore a whole backup over legitimate new work just to make checksums agree.

Measure optimization on a fixed synthetic workload before and after the change. Include typical and maximum supported history sizes; separate data preparation from LVGL rendering, disk writes and RF latency. Use warmups and report medians without fragile timing thresholds in tests. A headless benchmark can run on the actual device without opening its radio/camera/display, and should stay outside the installed app. Reduced work does not establish hours of battery life.

Do not use repeated sudo subprocesses as a long-running health-check transport. A timeout can make an unprivileged parent attempt to kill a now-elevated child, causing EPERM and leaving cleanup outside its control. A separate fixed-purpose capability service can own the privileged probe and publish an atomic verdict. Validate the record's owner, type, writable modes, boot identity and freshness; fail closed when it is absent/stale/false. Test the real service identity and actual rule changes, not just the JSON parser. Remove stale comments and privilege exceptions when the normal user process no longer needs escalation.

A linked dependency can also bring its own install rules into CPack.
