Wireless Surveyor's actual archive audit found LVGL development headers and its static library under shared include/lib directories, despite the app's own namespaced install rules. With the project's CMake 3.31 integration, declaring the LVGL FetchContent dependency EXCLUDE_FROM_ALL retained normal dependency linking and excluded those development payloads from the application installer. Verify the resulting archive and keep runtime licenses; an intent in CMake is not proof of package contents.

docs.title: Reduce installation friction without hiding dependencies
docs.text:
Prefer the official image's system facilities. Distinguish required OS packages, app-private components, optional peripherals and account setup. The current Store implementation uses APT for missing Debian dependencies: correct Depends can remove manual steps without copying system libraries into every app. Recheck that behavior, package availability and permissions on the supported image before relying on it.

For a dependency that needs a specific correction, an app-private runtime can avoid PATH drift and a competing system daemon. This is a deliberate option, not a requirement that every app use Python, a supervisor or bundled binaries. Pin original artifact hashes, supported ABI and source/patch revisions; retain licenses and paired corresponding source. Keep large generated dependency/source archives as release assets rather than committing build output into Git.

If preparing a user environment on first launch, make preparation offline, bounded and repeatable. Verify package-owned inputs, ignore inherited installer index/config overrides, lock concurrent preparation, recognize incomplete caches and repair only a fixed private cache. Keep existing user environments and app data untouched. A preinst interpreter belongs in Pre-Depends; ordinary dependencies may arrive too late. Never run a user environment as root or start hardware during install. Stop only the app's live service before replacing its modules; verify the newly started process afterward.

Test this in a minimal supported Debian container with no preinstalled SDK, global daemon or operator environment. Disable networking for first launch; check import/functionality, repeat launch, damaged-cache recovery, tampered input rejection and uninstall/data preservation. This complements a fresh-image device check; it cannot prove hardware permissions, display behavior or boot timing. If no spare card is available, record physical fresh-image testing as deferred and never erase the working device to turn a checklist green.

Offer a prebuilt installer plus paired source/dependency archive, simple install/build entry points and checksums. Give manuals separate checksum asset names so later uploads cannot replace installer verification. State which downloads remain: Docker/toolchains, OS packages and accounts are external. Offline builds need named caches/images prepared first; claim a zero-download first build only when supplied and tested.

docs.title: Document the operator's whole lifecycle
docs.text:
A dependency change is incomplete if only the code and release notes are updated. Keep one current operations runbook covering actual artifact availability, checksums, supported image, transfer/install, first launch, upgrade, private backup and deliberate restore, service/log recovery, compatible rollback and removal. State what is bundled, supplied by APT, optional or account-dependent. Keep dated evidence intact, but label obsolete commands and link to current instructions.

Generate an offline installer instruction asset from that runbook, and update the user manual's startup/recovery sections. Keep tested binary/source hashes fixed when refreshing documentation; give new document assets their own provenance/checksums and do not imply a documentation update requalified hardware. A draft is not a public download. Installation examples must not assume root launch, a developer's username, existing private environment or account secrets.

docs.title: 7. Radio bring-up (LoRa Cap)
docs.text:
Only relevant if your app drives the Cap LoRa-1262. This is the sequence to power and initialize its SX1262 robustly from userspace with no root. Getting it wrong is what defeated earlier attempts on this device, so it's worth doing carefully.

⚠️ Attach the antenna before powering the radio. Transmitting without an antenna can permanently damage the SX1262. The software cannot check this — it's on the user, so say so in your UI and docs.

docs.title: Confirmed wiring (this Cap on this board)
docs.text: Line Value SPI /dev/spidev0.1 (kernel CS1) RESET GPIO26 BUSY GPIO22 DIO1 / IRQ GPIO23 RF switch SX1262 DIO2 (DIO2_AS_RF_SWITCH=true) TCXO SX1262 DIO3, 3.0 V Cap 5 V rail /sys/class/leds/ext_5v_out/brightness (1 = on) EXT selector /sys/class/leds/ext_usb_gpio_fun/brightness — must be 0 (GPIO mode) Band-path expander PI4IOE5V6408 at I²C 0x43 on /dev/i2c-1 (lives on the Cap; only answers once the 5 V rail is up) GNSS /dev/serial0 @ 115200 (shares the 5 V rail)

docs.title: Run it in a child process
docs.text: Run the radio in a child process whose lifetime matches the connection, so the kernel frees every GPIO line and the spidev handle the instant it exits or crashes — no stuck pins, no lingering lock. Let the kernel be the lock: don't invent a lockfile for the SPI bus; a second claimant gets EBUSY and the kernel cleans up on exit. (This is the same child-process boundary the architecture chapter recommends for all hardware work.)

docs.title: The sequence (ordered)
docs.text:
1. Pre-flight. Check /dev/spidev0.1, /dev/gpiochip0, /dev/i2c-1 exist and are read/write; turn each failure into a specific message (no-spi / no-gpio / no-i2c / permission → "add your user to the spi, gpio, i2c groups and re-login"). If a known holder owns the radio (another LoRa app, a bridge), say so rather than retry-failing.
  2. Power, saving state first. Read and save the current ext_5v_out and ext_usb_gpio_fun values. Write ext_5v_out=1, then ext_usb_gpio_fun=0 (at =1 the Cap's reset line is cut and the chip stays in reset). Sleep ~100 ms for the regulator and the on-Cap expander to come up.
  3. Band path (the 0x43 expander). On /dev/i2c-1, address 0x43: verify the ID register first (expect 0xA2, maker bits 0b101); then write the output level (reg 0x05) before the direction (reg 0x03) so the RF-enable pin comes up already-high with no low glitch, then high-Z (reg 0x07). Classify every failure (busy / absent / wrong-chip) with an actionable message; on any failure here, restore the LED switches and abort cleanly.
  4. Init the SX1262. Let your radio library do the reset pulse, BUSY handshake, DIO3-TCXO (3.0 V), DIO2-as-RF-switch, and image calibration — don't hand-code them. Construct with: SPI spidev0.1, RESET 26, BUSY 22, IRQ/DIO1 23, DIO2_AS_RF_SWITCH=true, DIO3_TCXO_VOLTAGE=3.0. Filter constructor kwargs against the driver's real signature so a library version that doesn't accept a field doesn't crash you. begin() with a few retries and escalating backoff (~1.5 s) to ride out a line a dying prior process is still releasing.
  5. Serve / run. This is where your actual radio work happens — e.g. running meshtasticd against the now-powered Cap, which handles the SX1262 and the Meshtastic protocol via its YAML. The Cap power + the 0x43 band path are yours to do first, because the radio daemon does not drive them.
  6. Teardown on normal exit. In a try/finally: stop the radio, then restore ext_usb_gpio_fun and ext_5v_out to their saved values in reverse order (5 V rail back off, so the Cap doesn't drain the battery). This must run on a failed start. A finally block cannot run after SIGKILL; use a separate guardian and service cleanup for abrupt termination. Restore exact prior values; do not assume a saved rail value was zero.

docs.title: Gotchas (each one cost real debugging)
docs.text:
• ext_usb_gpio_fun must be 0, or the Cap's reset line is cut and the SX1262 stays in reset.
  • Power the rail and settle ~100 ms before touching the expander — it has no power before that, so probing it earlier reads a false "absent."
  • Write the expander's output level before its direction to avoid a low glitch on the RF-enable pin.
  • The radio library's IRQ-watch thread can stall shutdown ~2 s, but the launcher only allows ~3 s between SIGTERM and SIGKILL — stop the edge threads before cleanup or your app looks like it hangs on quit.
  • Resolve the gpiochip by its kernel label, not its number — the number can move across CM revisions and kernels.

docs.title: If you bundle a GPL radio daemon
docs.text:
The native daemon and Python client retain their GPL terms. Mesh's supervisor is GPL-3.0-or-later; its separate UI files retain their MIT terms. Preserve each component's applicable licenses and corresponding-source obligations. A process or socket boundary is not an automatic licensing exemption.

Earlier Mesh versions used separate prerequisites. Version 0.1.19 redistributes a private native runtime and locked wheels with notices and paired source. Neither plan is universal; see packaging and security/publishing.

docs.title: Legal/operational rules to surface in your app
docs.text:
• Use a band you're licensed to transmit on (e.g. 902–928 MHz in the US).
  • Antenna before power (above).
  • Support public channels deliberately and label them clearly. Use a secret random key for traffic that needs a private group; public default keys provide no group privacy.

Next: shipping it safely — security and publishing.

docs.title: Radio configuration is part of the safety boundary
docs.text:
The daemon can transmit from persisted settings during startup, before a client has connected and inspected them. Prepare a reviewed profile with the correct region before powering it, and document that boot window. Validate the effective per-channel location precision and MQTT module state, not just the broadcast interval. Do not enable position on every enabled channel: a public primary may have been deliberately disabled for location. Require an explicit channel target and verify real readback. A DM or trace must not silently use a public primary.

Validate persisted configuration before powering the device/daemon, not only after connecting. Firmware can emit identity or telemetry on its primary channel without a UI send intent. Distinguish an operator's private-only configuration from a product-wide restriction. A general client can support public and private channels while requiring explicit routing and separate location consent. Disable unapproved public location defaults before firmware can broadcast; persist only confirmed consent, bound to channel identity and precision. Preserve frequency/modulation when converting an existing secondary private channel into a private-only profile, and verify the peer link. Check the firmware's accepted preference schema and required fields too: an empty or stale protobuf may parse successfully but trigger factory defaults at boot. An absent transmission flag must not be mistaken for verified receive-only configuration. Fail closed for schemas your integration has not qualified.

Parsing a fresh protobuf is insufficient to validate first run. Explicitly set required operational defaults, then start the actual daemon from empty app state and read them back. A default-false security/console flag can suppress startup diagnostics even while the daemon runs. Likewise, an empty settings submessage may be serialized in every disabled channel slot; message presence alone does not prove that a slot contains a retained configuration. Check meaningful fields.

Verify requested settings semantically. Firmware can populate derived modem fields and normalize empty submessages, so whole-message byte equality can reject a successful change. Compare the requested effective values and safety invariants such as transmission state. Test both an accepted normalization and a genuine readback mismatch. Treat expected tuning reboots as a planned stop/reconnect, while preserving unexpected disconnects as actual failures.

Public and private chat channels share one radio's region, modem preset and frequency slot. Importing a channel key does not establish matching RF tuning. Expose those settings and avoid silently applying URL tuning or replacing an existing channel just because the names match. A DM must not choose an arbitrary private channel or fall back to the public primary when its selection disappears.

docs.title: Check kernel ownership, not only device-file permissions
docs.text:
Read/write access to /dev/gpiochip0 does not mean the needed lines are free. A different Cap's SPI overlay can claim a line through a kernel driver, with no userspace GPIO file descriptor to find. Query line ownership before power-on and surface the specific conflict. On this image, the NFC SPI-CS2 overlay reserves GPIO22, which LoRa needs for BUSY, and the upstream NFC app leaves the runtime overlay until reboot. Do not silently unbind another driver's pin or remove a shared SPI overlay; those actions can affect the display and other apps.

Normalize vendor sysfs values by their physical meaning. This image can report 255 for an enabled binary GPIO LED despite max_brightness=1. Validate the complete recovery record before writing any switch and persist canonical logical0/1, so valid vendor values cannot strand all later starts behind a failed recovery.

docs.title: 8. Security, licensing and publishing
docs.text: Publishing a device application is a trust transaction. Two things earn that trust: least privilege (it only touches what it says it does) and integrity/provenance (they can tell it's really yours and unmodified). This chapter is both — plus the specific hardening lessons from putting a real app through an independent security review.

docs.title: Least privilege
docs.text:
Most of your app should need no root at all — the device user is already in the gpio/spi/ i2c groups, so SPI/GPIO/I²C work unprivileged. Escalate only for the few things that truly require it (raw sockets, monitor mode, firewall rules), and do it narrowly. In order of preference:

  1. File capabilities (setcap) — e.g. cap_net_raw+eip on just the binary that needs raw sockets. No sudo, no root process.
  2. A scoped, sandboxed systemd unit — its own unit (not a child of your UI), started through a narrow policy, with User=<non-root> (or DynamicUser=yes), NoNewPrivileges, an empty CapabilityBoundingSet=, ProtectSystem=strict, DeviceAllow= only the device it needs.
  3. A root-owned validating wrapper — only where capabilities can't reach, and it re-validates every argument.

The publish tooling enforces the floor: a bundled service running as root is rejected. Never ship a blanket NOPASSWD: ALL. And resist the convenience trap of exposing an on-device root shell — fine for a personal tool, wrong for a trust-first published app. Prefer enumerated, validated actions.

When the app uses IPC, follow the architecture chapter: IPC carries intent, not mechanism. The unprivileged side sends a named action with validated data, never a command string; the privileged side maps that to one fixed, validated action and treats everything it receives as untrusted input.

docs.title: Hardening lessons from a real review
docs.text:
These are the things an independent review flagged on a real app — the non-obvious ones worth applying when the corresponding feature exists. A local utility needs no firewall, socket or radio daemon merely to satisfy this list:

  • Make network confinement a startup precondition. If a daemon binds all interfaces, choose one fixed port and establish a dedicated IPv4/IPv6 firewall rule before spawning it. A command run once is lost on reboot; ship boot integration and verify the actual rule before every start. Stop on a failed watchdog recheck. Never flush unrelated rules. Use a capability-limited oneshot service or another narrow privileged boundary; keep the UI unprivileged. A loopback firewall still permits local clients; disclose that trust boundary.
  • Check dependency autostart too. Installing a daemon package can enable a separate system service with a different API port. Mask that service before installation when the app must own its child daemon; check for conflicting enabled/running units before power-on. A firewall for your child port does not confine another instance on its default port.
  • Authenticate and exclusively own the socket. Use a real, UID-owned 0700 directory, a 0600 socket and peer-credential checks. Reject symlink directories and unexpected owners. Hold a kernel advisory lock before unlinking a socket; checking its owner alone does not prevent two instances replacing each other.
  • Bound bytes, allocations, work and time independently. Limit complete and unterminated frames, JSON depth/value/string counts, pending queue bytes and records, clients, retained history, active workers and request queues. A count limit alone can still retain hundreds of huge messages. Limit UI events per tick. Reject malformed UTF-8/JSON and non-finite or overflowing numbers. Validate field ranges before arithmetic/drawing; type checks alone are not enough.
  • Treat a partial write as a broken stream. A timeout can leave a JSON prefix in the peer's buffer; sending the next record on that stream corrupts framing. Close/reconnect on incomplete writes and report failure; never automatically replay radio or destructive actions. Put bounded writes on a worker with an absolute deadline, not on the LVGL thread. Suppress SIGPIPE.
  • Show confirmed effective settings. A click is a request, not proof. Keep privacy state Pending/Unknown through disconnects, rejected writes, readback failures and timeouts. Confirm against the device, not the library cache you just edited. Test the actual behavior of “Off”; an interval of zero may mean the firmware default rather than disabled.
  • Validate consequential actions at their owner. A different route or view must not bypass validation, target identity or consent. The RF-specific example is preserved in Mesh route validation.
  • Own descendants and hardware through abrupt death. Parent termination does not imply child termination or power restoration. Use a guardian/service control group, stop/reap the child before restoring switches, and test SIGKILL and failed startup. Do not kill arbitrary PIDs matching a config pathname.
  • Make reconnect snapshots true. Persist delivery changes in the authoritative session store, deduplicate retries, ignore stale attempt ACKs, and propagate deletion/retention changes to every client. Put a global bound on “keep all.”

The meta-lesson: have someone (or something) review it who isn't you, before you publish. An author is blind to their own omissions.

docs.title: No secrets, ever
docs.text:
• No keys, tokens, passwords, or private channel material in the repo or the .deb.
  • User secrets (e.g. a radio channel key) live in the user's config dir at runtime, created by the user — never committed, never baked into the package. Keep the simulator's sample/fixture data wholly synthetic (no real identities, coordinates, or ids).
  • Scan before every release: git grep -iE 'password|secret|token|BEGIN .*PRIVATE KEY', and grep for your own device name, hostnames, local IPs, and home paths before a repo goes public. Scan tracked files, reachable Git history, package contents and images. A clean text scan does not inspect a screenshot: replace real chats, names, coordinates and device IDs with synthetic fixtures. Deliberate public copyright/author attribution should remain; it is different from accidentally exposed user data.

docs.title: Licensing (including the MIT/GPL split)
docs.text:
• Choose and state a license up front, in the repo and shipped in the package (/usr/share/doc/<pkg>/LICENSE). Preserve the official Template's MIT license and copyright for reused code; choose an appropriate compatible license for your own additions rather than assuming every application must be MIT.
  • Mind dependency licenses. Inventory linked libraries, copied code, fonts, generated assets, helpers and bundled executables. Preserve their notices and satisfy their actual terms; a process boundary is not an automatic exemption. The Mesh licensing example records the MIT UI/GPL supervisor and external-dependency choices for that app.

GPL allows redistribution subject to its terms, including the applicable source obligations; not bundling a dependency is a distribution choice, not a GPL prohibition. See the GPLv3 text, sections 4-6. Ship the full notices for the libraries and generated font data actually included in your binary, including components bundled inside LVGL; preserving only your application's MIT license does not preserve their copyright notices.

docs.title: Integrity, attribution, and the Store gate
docs.text:
• Public source repo; build the published binary from it; tag releases, so a reader can match the downloaded .deb to a commit.
  • Publish the exact tested .deb, its SHA-256 and full source commit. The Store's submission manifest records SHA-256 and PR validation checks it before promotion. A checksum is not a developer signature, source-to-binary attestation or security review. The Store README describes a separate on-device registry download check using MD5; do not assume every installation path verifies the submission's SHA-256. Keep the trust in account, hosting, catalog and installed client explicit. Never curl … | sudo bash — ship an inspectable package and verify its published SHA-256 independently.
  • Ship attribution in the package: a LICENSE and a THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md naming every borrowed component with its source URL, exact reference commit, and full license text. Preserve truncated upstream license texts in full.
  • Declare the 7 permission flags truthfully and state plainly in your README what hardware and network your app uses and why. For a radio app, state the safety and legal rules outright.
  • Use the Store's hardware-video review as a forcing function: if it isn't polished and working on the device, it isn't ready.

docs.title: Pre-publish checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Complete the Store readiness checklist and save the non-publishing preflight result with exact policy/catalog revision.
  • [ ] Categories, title/share-code uniqueness, images, author/Maintainer and seven permission flags satisfy the current official metadata policy.
  • [ ] Allowed install paths, unit/executable names, udev, modes and maintainer scripts checked against the actual package and current Store policy.
  • [ ] Dependency plan documented; fresh supported image can install/run it and missing/incompatible dependencies fail clearly without starting hardware.
  • [ ] Public repo; binary builds from it; release tagged.
  • [ ] License chosen and shipped; GPL vs MIT split correct if you link a GPL library.
  • [ ] .deb on a GitHub Release with its SHA-256 listed.
  • [ ] Runs unprivileged; any privilege is capabilities or a scoped sandboxed unit, never blanket sudo; no root service.
  • [ ] For a private local daemon: verify intended listener confinement after boot and before startup, and stop on failed enforcement. For an intentionally remote service: authenticate and encrypt access according to its threat model. If using a Unix control socket, verify private ownership/peers; bound inputs.
  • [ ] No secrets in repo or package (grep clean); user secrets live in the user's config dir; fixtures synthetic.
  • [ ] app-builder.json permissions honest; README states what it touches and (for radio) the safety/legal rules.
  • [ ] LICENSE + THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md (source + commit + license) shipped in the package.
  • [ ] Real icon + real 320×170 screenshots; no TODO/placeholder text anywhere.
  • [ ] Regressions cover relevant failure paths: malformed input, failed saves, stale callbacks and navigation; add stalled/partial streams, parent death and reconnect checks when those facilities exist. Record irrelevant checks as not applicable.
  • [ ] Inspect the generated .deb, not only the source manifest: identity/version, native library dependencies, icon/launcher paths, helpers/services and modes.
  • [ ] Reviewed by someone who isn't you; verified on the device; ready to record the hardware video.

Keep three decisions separate: local checks pass, hardware/security evidence is complete, and the Store accepted the submission. The preflight reports unverified evidence even on success. A first-release video does not replace an independent review or prove all cold-boot/network/privacy failure paths.

Publish only after reviewing the concrete package/listing/video. Protect the publishing account and ~/.czdev/credentials; never include its token, device-flow code or a personal terminal session in logs, CI artifacts or demonstration video. Show synthetic chats/locations and no usable private channel QR/share URL.

That's the path, end to end. For the implementation and its explicit verification limits, read the worked example. Build something good.

For port-confinement tests, verify a control endpoint is reachable on the same address family/path. “Network unreachable” is not evidence of a firewall drop. When the physical LAN cannot route IPv6, isolated network namespaces can verify the device kernel's IPv6 filtering; report that separately from a physical LAN probe, and leave the untested path explicit.

docs.title: Useful diagnostics without an accidental data export
docs.text:
Build support exports from a small whitelist of health states, versions, ages and counts. Exclude raw logs, names, node/device identities, keys, share URLs, coordinates, message text and personal paths. Test the export with synthetic sensitive sentinel values and verify they cannot appear. A generic recursive redactor applied to a raw runtime dump is harder to reason about than selecting known safe fields.

Keep fixed failure categories for timed-out checks, failed commands, invalid data and changed protection rules; do not collapse them into one cause or echo raw stderr/configuration. Test that failed checks still fail closed. A later healthy check establishes recovery, not the cause of the earlier failure or proof of a fix.

Conversation history and named hardware profiles introduce new sensitive files. Use private owned directories/files, bound history and record counts, define retention and deletion behavior, and offer an explicit RAM-only choice. Describe logical deletion honestly: flash, WAL and backups may retain old bytes, and private permissions are not at-rest encryption. Never put runtime state into CI artifacts.

For messaging apps, history opt-out must cover metadata as well as message/draft text: conversation identifiers and pins can reveal contacts. Suppress new metadata writes, migrate older opted-out stores, and test raw rows after restarting. Retaining that state in the active RAM session is a separate, explicit policy.

When a privilege design changes, remove obsolete sudo grants from the package and verify their absence after a real upgrade. A documented manual diagnostic command is still a privilege grant; replace it with an unprivileged health read when a trusted capability-only monitor already supplies the needed evidence.

Keep strict validation ahead of idempotence checks. In Python, True == 1, so an unchanged-state shortcut can accidentally accept an invalid flag. Once validated, skip duplicate persistence/broadcasts while retaining durability for real changes, history opt-out semantics, row quotas and explicit synchronization barriers.

Uninstallation needs an audit of changes made outside the package manifest: generated services, setuid helpers, file capabilities, runtime data and installer caches. A capability applied through a virtualenv symlink can land on the shared system interpreter. Prefer narrow service capabilities; avoid elevating a shared interpreter. Back up private app data, remove only grants actually attributable to that app, and preserve shared dependencies, hardware configuration and groups needed by other applications.

docs.title: Official components and contribution decisions
docs.text:
The 2026-11-18 UI/shell evaluation recommends reusing the appropriate official page/runtime foundation and adapting its presentation. Custom palettes, menus and layouts do not require a replacement app-shell SDK. Preserve ownership, input and backend authority; evaluate behavioral changes separately from appearance.

The 2026-11-18 keyboard/input evaluation checks current official sources and supplements the historical comparison below. Use the official shared input backend when that runtime fits; adapt the Template's navigation subset for text-entry needs. A general replacement keyboard library is deferred. Existing prepared contribution pins remain unchanged.

Reviewed 2026-11-16. Start with the official implementation that fits your project. This is a source-level comparison, not a security certification or a promise that two different build systems/components can be exchanged unchanged.

docs.title: Concrete keyboard gap
docs.text:
At the reviewed Template revision, the native map returns only selected navigation/shortcut keys. The shared launcher already has all 32 symbol assignments. The opportunity is reliable integration into this Template, not inventing a new keyboard layout or alleging the official shared map is wrong.

An existing Template contribution also requests additional keys. Inspect its current state before proposing another upstream change. My prepared proposal records its exact base, scope, code provenance, tests and remaining qualification. It has not been submitted or accepted upstream.

docs.title: Evidence and limits
docs.text:
The shared repository contains targeted tests for keyboard/input lifetime, screen cleanup, configuration failure/rollback, process handling and other services. See its runner and implementation snapshot. Selected source/tests and its build workflow were inspected; the complete upstream suite and device/image matrix were not rerun for this comparison. Do not equate the existence of tests, a green build, official ownership or a large test count with blanket reliability. The Template's navigation demo and the broader shared SDK are different integration paths.

CMake/SDL and SCons/Kconfig do not automatically share build flags, input event formats, ownership or callback conventions. Review dependencies and licenses, match the actual image, and exercise the complete path used by the app. The BSP cross-build archive is a target sysroot; it is not by itself a ready-made app UI kit.

docs.title: When a separate library is justified
docs.text:
My personal library principles allow reusable preferences and deliberate design choices alongside demonstrated fixes. A component can be useful without establishing a defect in the official implementation.

Require a recurring need or deliberate shared preference, two unrelated applications that actually use the same interface, useful independent tests, documented supported versions, clear licenses and an owner for compatibility/security fixes. Prefer small source components with explicit versions initially. Avoid introducing a new system-wide service or mandatory runtime dependency without a measured need.

Current direction: preserve tested reuse and record the personal library's principles while maintaining the general guide and focused keyboard contribution. The principles do not create a standalone framework or change an app, launcher or device. Component extraction remains a separate implementation decision.

Guide index · Project sections

docs.title: Review package and Mesh maintenance
docs.text: The M5Stack review package separates Template integration from Mesh 0.1.11 maintenance. Both carry bounded-poll and owner-scoped hold cleanup tests, including unrelated-device teardown. It supplies exact source/patch hashes, reproduction steps, licenses and qualified evidence, plus the modular-supervisor rationale. Preparation does not submit a PR or qualify the Template physically. Current personal-library direction is recorded in the agreed principles.

docs.title: Worked-example provenance: Tick & Bell
docs.text:
Area Source and scope Device input and display Official pinned CardputerZero Template and LVGL; preserve the documented keyboard mapping and package/launcher layout. Home carousel Adapted from the approved Mesh presentation and motion; NFC Tools is the visual source for the position dots. Text-only battery Reuse the official Template device status reader. The guide pattern changes presentation only: plain text aligned at the right, no glyph. Reusable code The guide's position indicator separates the visual cue from the app's selected index. Demo application Tick & Bell's clock scheduler, date defaults, five original tones and test flows are independent example work, not APIs supplied by M5Stack or Apple.

The existing two-version device tutorial still uses Guide Counter; Tick & Bell is a separate example being tested on a device. The app is not submitted to the Store, and only its own behavior is qualified by its test records.

Deliberate departure or addition Why it exists Limit Right-aligned battery percentage instead of Template's battery glyph plus percentage Keep the exact percentage visible without spending two slots on the same status. Use the official reader, not guessed levels. No invented value when the device does not report one. Vertical-only submenu selection rather than sharing carousel left/right shortcuts The list is arranged vertically and horizontal movement has a different job on editable rows. Printed F/X can serve as a convenience outside editors. No change to the official key map itself. Mesh carousel with NFC-style position dots instead of copying either app's full home screen The wider active slot shows position even with wrapping, with a non-color cue. A small independent helper avoids importing an app's state and backend. One implemented consumer so far; reuse is not a claim of cross-app or per-device testing. A small foreground UI backed by a per-user timer service Closing the UI should not stop an awake device's timers and alarms. A single scheduler owns persistent state. No power-off or OS-suspend wake guarantee. This is Tick & Bell-specific, not required for other apps.

The first-device and troubleshooting walkthroughs explain the learning gaps at the steps where the guide adds something. See the short route for the official/adapted/contribution labels.

docs.title: The counter demo is installed. What went wrong?
docs.text:
Use this page alongside the first-device app walkthrough. Start with what you see. Check the same .deb you intended to install and change one thing at a time. A good desktop run is useful evidence, but it does not test APPLaunch, the device keyboard, or the libraries on the handheld.

Why add this page? The official tools describe build and submission requirements. This guide starts from the symptom on the handheld, because a valid package can still have a wrong launcher entry, an unresolved library, or different key behavior. The checks narrow the problem without reimaging the device or changing unrelated packages.

docs.title: No app icon in APPLaunch
docs.text:
On the CardputerZero, check the package and the files it owns:

dpkg-query -W -f='${db:Status-Abbrev} ${Package} ${Version} ${Architecture}\n' cp0-guide-counter-demo
dpkg-query -L cp0-guide-counter-demo | grep '/APPLaunch/'

Look for ii (installed), the version you intended, and an entry under /usr/share/APPLaunch/applications/ for Guide Counter. Open that package's .desktop file and check [Desktop Entry], Name, Exec, Icon, and Terminal=false. Confirm Exec resolves to this app's executable (not another app's) and Icon resolves relative to /usr/share/APPLaunch/. See the launcher contract. If the entry is wrong, fix the package source rather than editing launcher-owned files or borrowing another package's name.

docs.title: The icon is there, but the app closes immediately
docs.text:
Note the time, launch once from APPLaunch, and look only at the matching startup lines. From a terminal in your regular device session, use the launcher’s user unit:

journalctl --user -u APPLaunch.service --since '2 minutes ago' -n 25 --no-pager

If that produces nothing, confirm the launcher unit for your image with systemctl --user list-units --type=service. An empty log or an access error does not prove the app ran. Use the first relevant error: a missing path points to package layout; a named missing .so points to a runtime dependency. The launcher can hand off display and keyboard settings that an SSH command does not, so running the binary remotely is not an equivalent launch test.

For example, an earlier official Camera build expected libcamera.so.0.7, but the device image had libcamera 0.8. The startup error identified a library mismatch, not a broken sensor. Camera v1.0.4 documents its move to libcamera 0.8. That was a Camera fix, not a dependency of this counter. Don't symlink incompatible libraries to silence the message.

docs.title: It works on the desktop, but not on the device
docs.text:
On a machine with Debian package tools, inspect the artifact without installing:

dpkg-deb -f ./your-demo.deb Package Version Architecture Depends
dpkg-deb -c ./your-demo.deb

Check for arm64, the correct package and files, and dependencies intended for the supported device image. On the device, if file is available, use it on the executable resolved from Exec (not the .desktop file or the .deb). A native device executable should be an ARM aarch64 Linux ELF; if Exec points to a script, check its interpreter and the binary it invokes instead. An arm64 package label does not turn a desktop binary into a device build. See cross-building and packaging.

docs.title: Menus open, but the keys do the wrong thing
docs.text:
Start with a short single press and no locked modifiers. From About (the home screen), press 8 to open Counter. In Counter, try C (right) and Z (left), then tap Esc to go back. Test hold Esc separately on About to exit to the launcher; it is not the same as the short back press. If navigation works but the count doesn't change, record the screen and one key that failed before changing mappings. Use the official key map and input checks to compare simulator and hardware; don't turn a mapping issue into a permission fix.

If asking for help, share the package version and architecture, image version, screen, expected result, and one relevant error line with usernames, device or network identifiers, and personal paths removed. Don't post a raw journal or delete saved data while diagnosing. The steps here are inspection only; they do not require root, a factory reset, or an OS reflash.

docs.title: First app: build the official counter
docs.text:
Build the official Template, open its counter, change the greeting, then add a working reset action. Optional: build and inspect a device package. This is a learning example, not a new production utility or a Store-ready app. It needs no radio, account, Cap, Python backend or service.

The example uses the official Template's existing shell, input routing, themes, assets, model/viewmodel and screens. I deliberately reuse them rather than creating another starter framework. No keyboard patch is needed for this navigation-only example; full text entry is a separate input decision.

docs.title: 1. Prepare your desktop
docs.text:
Use a working C++17 compiler, Git, Ninja and CMake 3.31 or newer. Desktop builds also need SDL2, FreeType, PNG, JPEG, fmt and zlib development files. On macOS with Homebrew, the official Template instructions list these dependencies:

brew install cmake ninja sdl2 freetype libpng jpeg fmt zlib
git --version
cmake --version

Linux dependency names and the broader build paths are in chapter 6. Check the actual CMake version: a distribution's default package may be older than 3.31. Install dependencies as a separate, deliberate setup step; the Store preflight never installs them for you.

docs.title: 2. Get reviewed source
docs.text:
Official foundation: CardputerZero Template and its pinned LVGL dependency.

From a working directory of your choice, use new directory names:

git clone https://github.com/CardputerZero/Template.git first-counter
git -C first-counter checkout --detach 477fa6d217b683e3084c361a757f03dc8ca9f753
git clone https://github.com/lvgl/lvgl.git first-counter-lvgl
git -C first-counter-lvgl checkout --detach 85aa60d18b3d5e5588d7b247abf90198f07c8a63
cd first-counter
git rev-parse HEAD

These commands download source. The pinned revisions make the walkthrough repeatable; they are not a claim that newer upstream changes are unnecessary. Compare later revisions before adopting them. The LVGL revision is the v9.5.0 source used for this example. Keep upstream MIT notices and asset licenses.

docs.title: 3. Build and open the desktop example
docs.text:
Official foundation: Template presets, simulator, built-in counter and normal keyboard routing. The particular walkthrough and evidence below are the guide contribution.

For an Apple Silicon Mac:

cmake --preset darwin-arm64 \
  -DFETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_LVGL="$PWD/../first-counter-lvgl"
cmake --build --preset darwin-arm64-dbg --parallel 4
./build/darwin-arm64/Debug/template_app

The result is an SDL simulator window containing the device UI, not a Debian installer. Keep the terminal open to see startup errors. If configuration fails, check the first missing dependency and CMake version; do not solve a missing library by running the application as root.

For Linux x86-64, use linux-x86-64 and linux-x86-64-dbg instead, then run ./build/linux-x86-64/Debug/template_app. This alternative is supplied by the pinned official presets but was not freshly executed for this walkthrough.

Try the following in the focused simulator window or its virtual keyboard:

  1. On the first page, use 8 to open the counter.
  2. Use C/Right twice: the counter should show 2.
  3. Use Z/Left three times: it should stop at 0.
  4. Tap Esc to return. On the first page, 6 changes the theme.
  5. Reopen the counter; its value remains for this running session. Hold Esc on the first page to exit. A fresh process starts at 0.

These keys come from the pinned input router and navbar, not a guessed keyboard map. Check the specific counter shortcuts: the first page's 4–8 actions are not its counter-page controls.

docs.title: 4. Make one visible change
docs.text:
Guide exercise: Change one greeting in the official Template; the model and viewmodel are upstream.

Close the simulator. In src/model/base_model.cpp, change only the greeting returned by BaseModel::greeting() from Hello World to My first counter. Then rebuild and launch with the same commands from step 3. The first page should show the new text. Check both themes and return from the counter. git diff should show only that greeting change.

The path from action to pixels is small: the navbar calls a viewmodel action; counter_subject_ holds this demo's session value; ButterScreen binds its label to that subject. The greeting comes from the model, published by the viewmodel and bound on the first screen. The existing screen manager owns screen changes. You do not need another process to understand or extend this example.

This demo is not a durable counting application. Before relying on it for real work, define a maximum count, persistence/reset behavior and recovery from write failure. Its increment action is not bounded for indefinite use; do not confuse this short exercise with production acceptance testing.

docs.title: 5. Add a reset action
docs.text:
Guide contribution: Add one callback and input slot while keeping Template’s event path and display binding.

Now change behavior, not just text: pressing 6 on the counter page should set the count to zero. On the home page, 6 should still switch themes. The official example already routes this key and binds the label to the count, so there is no need to add a driver, create a new screen or redraw the label yourself. Close the simulator and make these edits in first-counter.

  1. Give the viewmodel an action. In src/viewmodel/base_viewmodel.h, add void reset_counter(); immediately above void increment_counter();. In src/viewmodel/base_viewmodel.cpp, add this above the existing increment method:
void BaseViewModel::reset_counter() {
    counter_subject_.set(0);
}
  1. Route the key on the counter page only. In src/platform/linux_input.cpp, find nav_key_to_index(). Inside the first switch, the one under if (nav_shortcut_mode), add this case. Leave the second switch (home page) as it is:
case '6':
    return 2;
  1. Connect slot 2 to the action. In src/view/widgets/navbar.h, add static void reset_counter_cb(lv_event_t* event); next to increment_counter_cb. In src/view/widgets/navbar.cpp, replace the middle entry (index 2) in butter_icons with {"", reset_counter_cb},. Add lv_obj_remove_event_cb(button->root(), reset_counter_cb); immediately above the existing line that removes increment_counter_cb. This cleans up the old handler when switching screens. Add this definition immediately above NavBar::increment_counter_cb():
void NavBar::reset_counter_cb(lv_event_t* event) {
    auto* view_model = static_cast<viewmodel::BaseViewModel*>(lv_event_get_user_data(event));
    if (view_model) {
        view_model->reset_counter();
    }
}

  1. Show people what to press. In navbar.cpp, change the size of kButterShortcuts from 3 to 4 and insert {"6", "Reset"}, between the Less and More entries. To keep all four hints readable on 320×170, shorten those two key labels from Z/Left and C/Right to Z and C. The arrow keys still work and remain in Help. In navbar.h, change the size of shortcut_key_labels_ from 3 to 4 so it has room for the new hint. In src/view/widgets/help_popup.cpp, change the size of kButterRows from 3 to 4 and insert {"6", "Reset to zero"}, between Decrease and Increase.

  2. Rebuild and try it. Run the same build and launch commands as step 3. Press 8 to open the counter, press C/Right twice, then press 6. You should see Counter: 2 change immediately to Counter: 0. Press C/Right once and Z/Left once to check the original controls. Tap Esc to go home and press 6 there: it should still change the theme. Check that the counter footer fits in both themes.

Follow the action you added: key → navigation slot → callback → viewmodel → counter label. If the reset appears in the footer but does nothing, check that the new key maps to index 2 in the first switch and that index 2 in butter_icons points at the reset callback. If the counter changes, the existing subject binding takes care of updating the label.

docs.title: 6. Build an arm64 package without using the device
docs.text:
Adapted: Reuse the Template packaging implementation; the pinned native ARM64 container recipe and package inspection are guide work.

Continue only if you need the device artifact now. Desktop build success does not produce an arm64 binary. Use a separate Debian 13 arm64 environment, such as an isolated container/VM; do not install build dependencies on your handheld for this exercise. Copy the Template and LVGL source into that environment as sibling directories named first-counter and first-counter-lvgl.

Install the build dependencies there, then work as an ordinary user:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install --no-install-recommends \
  build-essential cmake ninja-build dpkg-dev \
  libfreetype-dev libpng-dev libjpeg-dev libfmt-dev zlib1g-dev
uname -m
cmake --version
cd first-counter
cmake -S . -B build/arm64 -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DUSE_DESKTOP=OFF \
  -DAPP_USE_DRM=OFF -DCM0_SDK_ROOT=/ \
  -DCM0_ALLOW_FETCH_DEPS=OFF \
  -DFETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_LVGL="$PWD/../first-counter-lvgl" \
  -DAPP_INSTALL_SYSTEMD_SERVICE=OFF
cmake --build build/arm64 --parallel 4
(cd build/arm64 && cpack)
dpkg-deb --info dist/TemplateApp_0.2.1_rev1_arm64.deb
dpkg-deb --contents dist/TemplateApp_0.2.1_rev1_arm64.deb

uname -m must report aarch64 for this native arm64 recipe. / is the dependency root inside that Debian arm64 environment, not a macOS sysroot or a cross compiler setting. The package is written to the Template's dist/ directory. The command disables the optional system service: this foreground demo needs none. These commands explicitly compile reviewed source; they are separate from the non-executing Store preflight.

docs.title: 7. Inspect before installing or publishing
docs.text:
Check that the package architecture is arm64, the desktop entry has Terminal=false, and its executable is /usr/bin/template_app. You can inspect package content in an isolated environment without installing or running it. No system service should be included with the option used above.

Do not install this demo over an existing Template-based app. It still uses the Template binary, config, icon and metadata identities. A different display name alone does not prevent file collisions. To make a real app, first give the CMake project/executable, asset namespace, desktop/icon paths, config path, Debian identity and app-builder.json coherent unique names. Replace placeholder maintainer/store data, preserve licenses, check actual runtime dependencies, and follow app anatomy and Store readiness. The demo's placeholder maintainer is intentionally not a real person's identity.

For the next hands-on step, use the separately named first device app instead of installing this Template artifact. The packaging chapter covers the general release checks. A device check should verify the exact installed artifact; no flashing or radio changes are needed for a counter. Store acceptance is a later, separate step.

docs.title: Verification and limits
docs.text:
Maintainer check on 2026-11-22, using the pinned sources above:

  • macOS arm64 desktop Debug build succeeded. Headless SDL startup remained alive for three seconds and exited cleanly when terminated. That is a startup smoke check, not the interactive sequence in step 3.
  • The greeting edit was rebuilt successfully; the diff and compiled executable contained the new text. Visual confirmation remains a reader check.
  • Debian 13 arm64 Release build and CPack packaging succeeded in a network-disabled container using already provisioned build dependencies. Package control/payload inspection confirmed arm64, foreground desktop entry and no systemd service or install/remove maintainer scripts. No package was installed on a device.
  • A fresh dependency installation/container-image build, Linux desktop run, manual end-to-end walkthrough, physical keyboard check and independent-reader exercise remain unperformed here.

Why add this exercise? The official Template shows a counter and its normal controls. The guide adds one feature so a beginner can follow an input all the way to the model and display without writing a new app framework. The unchanged Home shortcut is part of the test because keys should not change meaning outside the current screen.

The reset extension was checked separately in a temporary pinned Template copy on Apple Silicon. The Debug build succeeded. Synthetic desktop input exercised the simulator's normal event handler: opening the counter, going from 0 to 2, resetting to 0, incrementing and decrementing again, going back, and switching the home theme with the same key. The counter footer was visually inspected at 320×170 in both themes. The reset extension was not installed on a device; the arm64 package above was verified for the greeting edit, not the reset extension.

The source/package checks show that the example can compile and package in those specific environments. The evidence record pins the source, one-line edit, tool versions and inspected package hash. They do not prove that a new reader can follow it unaided, that a renamed app is release-ready, or that any peripheral works.

Short route · Choose the next capability

docs.title: First device app: install and update a saved counter
docs.text:
This optional exercise follows the simulator counter. It uses the same official Template and adds a separate app, Guide Counter, with two pages: About and Counter. It stores one number. It needs no Cap, service, network access at runtime, or Store account. This is a teaching package, not a Store submission. The unmodified Template package from the first tutorial is not the package to install here.

Desktop simulator captures using the official Template (MIT), not photos of the device.

Official: Template display, input, assets and Debian packaging foundation. Guide contribution: the independently named saved counter patch, its two teaching versions, and the install/upgrade/rollback tests. Neither version is an official Template release.

Why extend the official route? Template and AppBuilder explain how to build and package. This exercise connects those commands to a first real install, a launcher check, and an update with data to protect. A separate package name avoids overwriting a Template app. Two versions deliberately keep the same saved format so the reader can distinguish a working install from a safe update and rollback.

docs.title: 1. Build both versions and inspect the packages
docs.text:
Use the demo source and build recipe. Build version 0.1.0 and version 0.2.0 in separate build directories. Keep both packages. Use the desktop simulator to find About and Counter if this is your first build, but use the arm64 Debian packages for the rest of this page.

From a directory containing just the two artifacts, inspect each one before copying it to the handheld:

for file in ./*.deb; do
    dpkg-deb -f "$file" Package Version Architecture Depends
    dpkg-deb -c "$file"
    sha256sum "$file"
done

Both should report the same package name, cp0-guide-counter-demo, and architecture arm64, but different versions. Check that the launcher entry, executable, and shared launcher icon have demo-specific names. This demo should not install a service. A package built for the desktop or with the old Template identity is not interchangeable. Save the hashes so you can tell which files you tested. If macOS lacks these tools, run this check in the Debian build environment.

docs.title: 2. Install version 0.1.0 and try the physical keys
docs.text:
Use a spare microSD already running a supported Cardputer Zero image, or a device you have permission to change. Flashing a card erases its contents; nothing in this exercise requires rewriting a working card. Copy the two exact packages to a new folder in your home directory using your normal transfer method. On the device, verify the copied hashes and check for a collision:

dpkg --print-architecture
dpkg-query -W -f='${db:Status-Abbrev} ${Version}\n' cp0-guide-counter-demo

Expect arm64. On a first install the second command should report that no package matches. The state file is named in step 3. If you find an existing package or leftover demo state, do not install over it blindly. Use a fresh test account or a spare card, or deliberately preserve that earlier copy first.

Open a device terminal in the folder with both packages. For each install command below, use the exact file from step 1 and keep the leading ./. Use apt for the package install, but launch the app as your ordinary user, not with sudo.

sudo apt install ./cp0-guide-counter-demo_0.1.0_rev1_arm64.deb
dpkg-query -W -f='${Version}\n' cp0-guide-counter-demo

If APT proposes removing other packages or changing unrelated installed packages, answer No and check the troubleshooting page. Return to the launcher and open Guide Counter. Check the version in About. Press 8 to open Counter, then C/Right to add one and Z/Left to subtract one. Tap Esc to go back; hold Esc on About to exit to the launcher. Set the count to 3, close the app, and reopen it. It should still show 3. That last check uses a new process; switching screens alone would not test saving.

docs.title: 3. Upgrade without losing the count
docs.text:
Exit the app before installing a different version. Record the current count, then copy the demo's state file to a new private backup. Run these as the same ordinary user who opened the app:

state="${XDG_STATE_HOME:-$HOME/.local/state}/cp0-guide-counter-demo/count"
test -f "$state" && backup=$(mktemp "$HOME/guide-counter-backup.XXXXXX") &&
    cp -- "$state" "$backup" && printf 'Demo backup: %s\n' "$backup"

If the file is missing or the backup fails, stop and find out why before upgrading. Keep the old package and backup. The app owns only this one number; there is no schema migration in this exercise.

sudo apt install ./cp0-guide-counter-demo_0.2.0_rev1_arm64.deb
dpkg-query -W -f='${Version}\n' cp0-guide-counter-demo

Launch from the menu again. Check that About shows 0.2.0 and Counter still shows 3. Add one, close, reopen, and check 4. The version check and the saved-count check answer two different questions: whether you are running the new app, and whether it kept your data.

docs.title: 4. Roll back the app, then remove it
docs.text:
Exit the demo. Back up its current count separately using the step 3 command if you want to keep it. This tutorial's older build reads the same file format, so no restore should be needed. Ask APT first what the downgrade would do:

apt -s install --allow-downgrades ./cp0-guide-counter-demo_0.1.0_rev1_arm64.deb

Only if it proposes the demo downgrade and no unrelated changes, repeat with sudo apt install --allow-downgrades (without -s; do not add -y). Launch it again, verify 0.1.0 and 4, and then exit. A real application might change its file format; retaining an older package does not by itself make downgrading its data safe. If this demo fails to reopen, keep both saved copies and diagnose before restoring anything.

Use apt -s remove cp0-guide-counter-demo to preview removal; proceed with sudo apt remove cp0-guide-counter-demo only if the demo is the sole removal. Verify the launcher entry is gone and the user-owned state file still exists. The package manager should not erase your home-directory data. Leave that file in place unless you deliberately want to delete the exercise data.

docs.title: What to record
docs.text:
Note the image version, both package hashes, and which steps you performed: install, first launch, physical keys and exit, restart, upgrade, rollback, and removal. A desktop or container run is valuable but does not certify the physical screen, keys, or launcher. Mark those checks pending unless you performed them on a real device. See the recorded checks. A second person following the instructions unaided is a separate reader check.

Symptom-first troubleshooting · Packaging reference

docs.title: Try the guide on your own
docs.text: This is a usability check of the instructions, separate from testing an app. Give a new builder the short route and counter walkthrough, without this project's chat history. Let them choose a supported desktop environment. No device or private credentials are needed for the first build.

docs.title: What to record
docs.text:
• Guide Git revision, operating system/architecture, compiler and CMake versions.
  • Which route they followed and whether they found the correct dependency list.
  • Whether they could build, locate the executable, open the counter, change the greeting and rebuild without unwritten assistance.
  • Optionally, whether they could add the reset action from the walkthrough and confirm that the same key still changes the theme on the home screen. Record this separately from the first-build result.
  • The first instruction that was unclear, its expected result and what happened.
  • Whether they understood the difference between a desktop build, an arm64 package, physical testing and a publishable app.
  • Whether they could find the next recipe for their own idea without reading every peripheral chapter.

Do not collect private paths, network names, account details or complete logs without reviewing/redacting them. A short error excerpt and tool versions are usually enough. Do not install a template package over another developer's app.

docs.title: How to run the check
docs.text:
Ask the builder to explain what they expect before each milestone. Record help provided, including any missing command supplied by the observer; a rescued step is not an independent success. Time spent is useful context, not a performance target. Stop on an unexpected privilege request, package collision or hardware instruction unrelated to the chosen route.

Finish by asking: What could you skip? What did you read twice? What would you build next, and which chapter would you open? Fix the instruction at its primary home and retest the confusing step with a fresh reader when possible.

docs.title: Differences to decide together
docs.text:
These are preferences to resolve, not defects established by this inventory:

  • Color: parameterize burgundy and amber; choose defaults per app.
  • Supporting text: Surveyor's 12 px helper and NFC's 10 px details differ. Choose a baseline using real 320×170 examples before enforcing consistency.
  • Footer content: Mesh's contextual/action-oriented footer and Surveyor/NFC's navigation hints differ. Decide which help belongs in the footer versus Help, preserving useful actions and space for content.
  • Selection: list selection uses a left rail/fill; Mesh message bubbles have their own red outline. Treat these as distinct semantic states.
  • Architecture: background lifetime and hardware authority determine the process model. Visual consistency does not require identical backends.

docs.title: Proposed version 0.1
docs.text:
This is a candidate scope, conditional on reviewing current official guidance and implementations first. The inventory's older official source pins are historical comparison evidence, not completion of that current review.

Keyboard evaluation completed: the official-input review recommends the official backend for shared-runtime apps and a focused adaptation for Template text-entry apps. A standalone keyboard library is deferred. The UI/shell evaluation recommends official foundations with personal presentation adapters and defers a replacement shell. Other candidates still need their own official evaluation. For input, define the Template integration profile and compare it with the shared-runtime path before deciding whether versioned code or guidance/tests best meets my needs.

If justified by that evaluation, the first implementation should be small enough to adopt and compare safely:

  1. Keyboard/input package: the identical MIT decoder, official-map provenance, independent fixture, and reconciled regression harness. Document the evdev integration contract and app-specific adapters; do not assume their current reader implementations are interchangeable.
  2. Design reference: named color roles, app palette variants, type/spacing decisions, selection examples and navigation/footer conventions. Resolve the open preferences above before treating them as defaults.
  3. Integration example: a small Template-based editor/list example using the existing prepared contribution where suitable, with fake input and no hardware acquisition. This can be a development fixture, not another installed app.
  4. Architecture recipes: Mesh's persistent owner, Surveyor's bounded worker and NFC's fixed helper as alternatives, including costs, authority and cleanup.

Carousel and list widgets are the next code candidates after the input component has a stable interface. They need extraction work; this inventory does not call them ready-made drop-in components. Avoid including complete app controllers, radio/NFC operations, privilege rules, storage schemas or network-service adapters in the initial general package.

docs.title: Extraction and acceptance gates
docs.text:
• First evaluate current official guidance and implementation for each candidate; record source revisions, fit, limitations and the use/adapt/depart decision. Recurrence in my apps alone does not settle that decision.
  • Preserve M5Stack and other notices. Inspect file-level licenses and dependencies; NFC's GPL-marked UI/core and Mesh's GPL supervisor are not automatically MIT because other files or the communication boundary are MIT. Prefer an existing appropriately licensed source and review terms before copying or distribution.
  • Use immutable source snapshots. NFC's uncommitted work must be stabilized or explicitly snapshotted before it becomes a library baseline.
  • Retain independent expected input vectors and actual evdev/editor tests; add lifecycle/focus/animation tests for extracted UI. Historical app passes alone do not qualify a new package or its integrations.
  • Adopt one component at a time in an existing app, compare behavior and both-theme rendering, then verify another consumer. Keep app-specific behavior and state.
  • Document supported LVGL/build/input versions, ownership and update procedure. Investigate official changes before maintaining a separate implementation.
  • Discuss each meaningful departure and any proposed upstream sharing under the library principles. No upstream submission is implied.

docs.title: Personal reusable-library principles
docs.text:
Recorded 2026-11-18. The component inventory applies these principles to existing app code and proposes the first implementation scope.

My library captures how I prefer to build applications for CardputerZero: their appearance, interaction and internal design. It preserves tested work and lessons so future apps can be more consistent and easier to build and maintain. These principles describe my choices; the general app guide continues to distinguish platform requirements from optional approaches and personal preferences.

docs.title: Build on the official foundation
docs.text:
Use suitable official firmware, components, tools and documentation as the starting point. The library complements that foundation. Reuse and adapt what works well, preserve attribution and licenses, and add pieces that serve my apps. Its purpose is not to replace official firmware or official app-building guides.

Before designating any piece as reusable or designing its extraction, first inspect the relevant current official guidance, implementation and examples. Record the reviewed versions, what they provide and how they fit my needs. Then decide whether to use the official approach as provided, adapt it or deliberately take a different approach. Document the reasons, tradeoffs and compatibility implications. Existing shared code in my apps is a candidate, not an automatic decision to maintain my own implementation. Apply this order to visual components, input, application logic and backend patterns alike.

docs.title: Preserve preferences and deliberate design choices
docs.text:
UI preferences should normally be expressed through styling, layout and focused view components on the official foundation. Preserve the selected shell's lifecycle/input/resource contracts and backend authority. If a preference also changes behavior, identify and discuss that effect rather than assuming it is cosmetic. The official UI evaluation records this boundary and the components already available.

Reusable work can include layouts, colors, spacing, menus, highlighting, keyboard behavior and navigation. It can also include specific application logic, persistence, background work and backend organization.

A component does not need to correct an official defect to belong in my library. It may express a preference or a deliberate architectural choice. Mesh's modular UI/backend design is one example: I chose separation to suit its responsibilities and make parts easier to maintain and test, accepting additional communication and coordination. Record why a pattern was chosen, its benefits and costs, and when it fits. Each new app should use the pieces appropriate to its needs; modularity does not require every app to have Mesh's supervisor architecture.

docs.title: Investigate differences fairly
docs.text:
I may intentionally choose a different approach from the official developers. Before calling it a fix or improvement, inspect the relevant official design and version, check whether the concern has already been addressed, and consider whether the difference reflects an intentional choice or different requirements.

When claiming a better approach, identify the use case and demonstrate the benefit. Test the behavior, document tradeoffs and compatibility, and separate what has been verified from what remains uncertain. Official origin alone does not establish that an approach is best for every app; my preference alone does not establish a general improvement.

docs.title: Decide what to keep or share
docs.text:
I review meaningful departures to decide what they represent:

Kind of contribution How I treat it Personal preference Keep it as part of how I build my apps. Useful alternative Document its reasons, tradeoffs and situations where it fits. Demonstrated improvement or fix Consider sharing the evidence and implementation with the official developers.

These categories can overlap. A difference does not automatically require an upstream proposal, and a personal choice may still be useful to others. I decide case by case whether to keep it within my library, document an optional approach or share it with M5Stack. Recording or preparing work does not make that sharing decision for me.

docs.title: Keep reuse practical
docs.text:
Prefer focused, tested components and understandable patterns. Preserve useful lessons, supported-version information and ownership expectations as pieces are reused. Extract shared code when actual use supports it, while continuing to use official components that fit. A shared library should reduce repeated work and support reliability without forcing unrelated apps into one design.

docs.title: What the official approach provides
docs.text:
Guidance: hold/one-shot/lock modifier behavior and Fn actions are already specified. Bare F/Z/X/C as arrows outside text entry is an official recommendation, not a new layout invented by my apps. The specification recommends aligned 4–8 action hints and also allows other keys with visible explanations. My footer preferences should be evaluated against that guidance during visual design; they are not a reason to alter the physical keymap.

Template: map_evdev_key() at lines 186–215 handles Escape, Left/Right, Z/C, 4–8, Screenshot and Help. It is a navigation subset, not a complete text-entry adapter: ordinary letters and the full Sym map are absent. A text-heavy app scaffolded from it still needs input integration. AppBuilder copying the latest Template does not add that missing behavior. This is an integration limitation for my use case; the review does not establish that the demo's scope was accidental.

Shared runtime: keyboard_input.h supplies physical key identity, Unicode/ UTF-8, modifiers, press/release/repeat and semantic input context. It exposes a key filter before application/native keypad delivery and optional keypad interception. The context-scope helper restores the preceding context. The navigation contract aliases F/X/Z/C outside text mode. Its device implementation uses xkbcommon and compose; it also supplies a Cardputer-specific default map and runtime map loading. The default map still has all 32 expected assignments, including code 92 as slash.

Applications must distinguish native LVGL navigation events from the structured keyboard event, and must not retain the borrowed event object. Consume decoded text at that API boundary; sending it through another raw decoder would apply translation twice. The prepared decoder’s LVGL/special-action values are not interchangeable with the shared backend's evdev/keysym/semantic fields.

Build and ownership: this shared implementation is source integrated through SCons/Kconfig with dependencies including libinput/xkbcommon/udev. It is not a header-only replacement for the Template's CMake reader. An installed launcher does not automatically supply its internal input objects to a separate app. Migration needs deliberate build, event, lifecycle and dependency integration.

Keyboard Guide: useful for diagnosis and understanding image-dependent modifier reporting. It includes sysfs, legacy I2C and evdev fallback behavior. That diagnostic role does not make direct modifier-register access necessary for normal text input. Do not copy its legacy I2C ownership into every app.

docs.title: Use, adapt or depart
docs.text:
Area Recommendation Reason and boundary Physical symbols and Fn assignments Use official Complete guidance/map exists. The independently checked fixture matches it; no evidence justifies a competing map. New shared-runtime app Use official backend; adapt app callbacks Rich decoded input/context/filter APIs already exist. Keep my visual preferences above that boundary. No separate decoder alongside it. Existing Template/CMake apps Adapt Template The native subset does not satisfy text entry. Retain existing qualified integration while evaluating a focused source extension and its tests. Avoid a broad architecture migration merely to eliminate repeated files. Portable decoder Candidate focused extension, not yet a new library It isolates raw-event translation for Template consumers and already has three identical copies. Central versioning might reduce maintenance, but it must retain provenance/tests and justify its integration cost. Broader layouts and composition Evaluate official xkb path The generic profile in the proposal is US-oriented and the symbol loader expects the complete known map. It is not feature-equivalent to xkb composition or arbitrary UTF-8 remapping. Shortcuts, editor focus, Help and menu controls Adapt per app Official contexts/filtering provide foundations; the app owns whether an action is available, consumed or restored after an overlay. A wholesale alternative keyboard subsystem Defer This review finds no demonstrated need to replace the shared runtime. No intentional departure is selected at that level.

This recommendation is conditional on the app's chosen build/runtime, not a rule that every app must use SCons, a supervisor or a different firmware image.

docs.title: Verification and limits
docs.text:
• Compiled and ran four unmodified selected official tests on macOS arm64 with ASAN/UBSAN, warnings as errors: input creation/deletion lifecycle, keyboard thread lifecycle, keyboard UTF-8/semantic navigation/queue contract, and nested input-context restoration. All passed; leak detection was disabled.
  • Independently compared the 32 defaults in the current official keymap source with the previously captured vendor fixture in Mesh; all code/name pairs match.
  • Inspected Template mapping/reader, shared headers, text helpers, delivery/filter path, queue, device reader, build selection, relevant tests, guidance and diagnostic source. This is a focused evaluation, not a full SDK security audit.
  • No complete SDK build/suite, Linux xkb runtime, actual raw-reader-to-editor integration or physical keys were newly qualified. Existing app tests and installed-device checks do not qualify a future shared component migration.
  • The reviewed shared queue push allocates nodes without an explicit cap in that function. Do not assume the entire input pipeline is bounded simply because it is official; producer/consumer behavior needs evaluation before adopting it. This observation is not a demonstrated whole-system failure or an upstream fix.
  • No app source, device, source pins for the prepared contribution, firmware or publication state was changed. Downloaded sources and test binaries/logs stay in ignored build storage; only report/evidence metadata is recorded here.

docs.title: Next implementation decision
docs.text:
First document a Template input integration profile: required behaviors, boundary between decoder and reader, callback/focus ownership, supported versions and tests. Reuse the existing prepared example where it fits. Compare that profile with a shared-runtime integration example before deciding whether the personal library needs a versioned Template extension or only integration guidance and tests. No extraction or migration is authorized by the existence of this report alone.
