docs.title: Two meanings of shell
docs.text:
The device launcher discovers/launches applications and coordinates display, input and timers while handing control to an external process and returning. An app's theme should not replace that process policy or duplicate its global controls. Internal launcher pages and independent packaged apps are different integration paths.

The app's own UI foundation owns its screen, focus group, content regions, widgets and callbacks. The Template supplies a CMake/MVVM path; the shared cp0 runtime supplies a SCons/Kconfig runner/page path. Choose a coherent path for an app. Neither path requires copying the launcher's whole home screen, settings tree or hardware service selection into every application.

docs.title: What the official code already supports
docs.text:
• Template ScreenManager defers page requests with LVGL asynchronous work, cancels pending work and removes its observer during destruction. BaseScreen owns the screen and its title/navigation widgets. These mechanisms already provide useful ownership; custom menu styling does not require a new manager.
  • Template theme roles separate surfaces, text, buttons and semantic status colors. Theme bindings observe changes through object-associated observers. This is a suitable foundation for app palette variants and styled widgets.
  • Shared AppPage is the standard content/top-bar page. AppPageRoot explicitly supports a blank/custom page, and the API supplies optional bottom-bar layout and separately owned title/time/network/battery components. Custom content is an intended use, not inherently a departure from the official architecture.
  • Shared runner hooks separate setup, quitting and teardown from the app's page content. The HelloWorld example uses that runner while owning its own controls and palette state.
  • Official APPLaunch has carousel and settings selector implementations. They are examples with launcher-specific dependencies, not evidence that every native app must use that exact presentation or can import it unchanged.

docs.title: Use, adapt or depart
docs.text: Area Decision What can change and what must stay compatible App loop, screen ownership and teardown Use the selected official foundation Retain one coherent initialization/input/render/cleanup path. Do not add a second runner to obtain a different appearance. Existing apps need no migration solely for visual uniformity. Screen transitions and Back Adapt app navigation above that foundation Page names, menu order and navigation depth belong to the app. Preserve safe deferred destruction, pending-work cancellation and focus restoration. Colors and selection Adapt palette/styles Burgundy, amber, rounded rows, left rails and bubble outlines can differ by app and state. Keep focus distinguishable and errors understandable without relying on color alone. No source-level need to retain the demo accent was found. Fonts, spacing and geometry Adapt within measured content bounds Template uses 30 px title/footer constants; shared page API has a 20 px standard top bar. Those are implementation defaults, not one universal visual mandate. Derive usable content size from the selected layout and verify full font height, long text and selected-row visibility at 320×170. Top/status bar Reuse/adapt supplied components Customize title and placement using the chosen page API. A blank page or disabled bar is supported by the shared API; if status is shown, its source and meaning must stay truthful. Detach subscriptions/timers before destroying associated objects. Footers and actions Adapt with documented key choices Official guidance recommends aligned 4–8 action hints and also permits other keys with explanations. My contextual actions and reduced navigation hints are preferences to review, not automatically incompatible. Keep actual shortcuts and displayed actions consistent, and preserve Help access. Carousel Use official examples as references; adapt presentation APPLaunch's five-slot geometry, images, slider and registry are launcher-specific. I can keep my lightweight app carousel style without transplanting the entire launcher. A later reusable widget needs item/callback and ownership boundaries plus lifecycle tests. Lists and settings menus Evaluate/adapt existing examples APPLaunch already has a settings roller with centered selection, long-text scrolling and focus changes. Its settings-tree/font/component dependencies differ from a simple app list. Compare those dependencies before extracting another list implementation. Row style does not justify importing global setting actions. Help, toast and progress Reuse/adapt Template widgets where suitable Supply app content, dimensions and font choices; keep timer/observer cleanup. Help must own input while open. Keep transient/persistent messages distinct and show real operation state rather than optimistic success. Screenshots and overlays Adapt capture integration if needed Template parents Help/Toast to the top layer while its screenshot service snapshots the active screen. An overlay screenshot therefore needs an explicit capture/parenting decision. This is an integration concern, not a demonstrated firmware defect. App settings and backend state Preserve authority; adapt only presentation Theme or menu changes must not implicitly toggle device-wide services, change radio settings, write tags or alter privacy. Global Settings views are not harmless style components. Keep app preferences separate from backend-confirmed state. Background work and modularity Keep the app-appropriate architecture A custom palette does not require changing Mesh's supervisor, Surveyor's worker or NFC's helper. Respect the chosen LVGL thread/locking boundary; return background results through the app's established UI handoff. A replacement app-shell SDK Defer Both official foundations already accommodate custom presentation. Reuse the foundation first; justify any additional component by a specific need and compatible integration.

docs.title: How visual preferences will be recorded
docs.text:
For each preference, record the desired appearance, applicable states, official component used, styling/layout adaptation and behavior that must remain intact. Examples include an accent palette, selected-row rail, readable supporting text or an action-oriented footer. These can become theme data, layout parameters, focused widgets or documented patterns; they do not all require new classes.

Changes that hide essential feedback, make an action ambiguous, break focus, trigger commands twice or change consent/save behavior require a behavior review. Discuss any resulting tradeoff with the owner. Existing app differences are inputs to that discussion, not silently approved universal defaults. In particular, the inventory's footer and type-size choices remain open.

docs.title: Checks performed and limits
docs.text:
• Reviewed current official sources and examples at the revisions above; retained hashes in the evidence manifest. No claim is made that all SDK services or all official apps were reviewed.
  • Four unmodified official helper-contract tests pass on macOS arm64 with ASAN/UBSAN and warnings as errors: screen-component detach, screen-delete cleanup, status-resource readiness and runner lifetime/concurrent claims. Leak detection was disabled. These test helper behavior, not rendered screens, physical keys, complete teardown under every fault or a race-free runtime.
  • No new app build, full SDK suite, pixel/layout rendering, device qualification, live backend operation, extraction, migration or upstream submission occurred. Downloaded source and test binaries/logs remain in ignored build storage.
  • Source/license notices remain applicable to later copying. This report does not establish that every launcher-local example is a stable public component.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text:
Record the owner's visual and interaction preferences against this boundary matrix, then prepare a small style specification with representative screens and states. Resolve footer/type/selection choices before enforcing consistency. After that, identify the smallest theme or widget adapters needed on top of the official foundation. Implementation and app migrations remain separate work.

docs.title: Build your first app
docs.text: You do not need to read the entire guide before building. Start with a small working screen, then add the facilities your idea actually needs. This route is for CardputerZero running Debian, not the ESP32 Cardputer or Cardputer ADV.

docs.title: The short route
docs.text:
1. Define one useful task. Write down what the user can do, what data survives closing, and whether any hardware or network access is required. A local counter needs neither a supervisor nor a setup wizard.
  2. Build the official starting point. Follow the counter walkthrough. It takes you from pinned source to a desktop build and an inspectable arm64 package. No device is needed yet.
  3. Make it yours. Change the greeting, then try the counter reset exercise. Rebuild and check both changes in the simulator. Follow a key press through the viewmodel to the screen before replacing any of the Template's structure.
  4. Choose only relevant extras. Use the table below. Read the linked recipe when adding that capability; the recipe is not a requirement for every app.
  5. Try it on a handheld (optional). The first-device walkthrough gives a separate saved counter its own package identity, then checks physical controls, upgrade and rollback.
  6. Prepare a real app for release. Give it its own identity, handle errors, preserve attribution, and follow build/install checks and security/publishing. A successful build is a starting point, not a release certificate.

Stop after the greeting if you only want a first working example, or do the reset exercise to add a feature of your own. The fuller reference is there when the next design question arises.

docs.title: Which sections do I need next?
docs.text: Your next need Read next Another local screen, a timer, calculator or game Local utilities; UI Notes, saved records, drafts or conversations Persistence/messaging; identity and durable intent Keyboard text entry Keyboard; evaluate the official input path before adding a decoder A website, network service or remote-control connection Networking; security GPS, camera, NFC, LoRa or another peripheral Project selector; use the specific peripheral recipe Playback or recording Audio/media Slow work or more than one resource owner Architecture choices; a separate service is one option A Debian installer, upgrade or Store listing Packaging; Store readiness

docs.title: Understand the labels
docs.text:
Platform requirements describe the device, launcher and packaging contract. Project recipes apply only to the facilities you use. Personal UI preferences record my chosen appearance and interaction; they are not official requirements. Case studies record what a particular project taught me, with its own test limits.

Start by inspecting official guidance and code. Reuse what fits; adapt what your app needs. Record the reason for a departure before treating it as a reusable improvement. The component comparison and library principles explain this distinction.

docs.title: Follow the source as you build
docs.text:
Label What it means Official M5Stack/CardputerZero source or instructions. Where a build is reproduced, follow the linked revision rather than assuming the latest code is the same. Adapted A named upstream or project pattern reused with changes. The guide names the source and the difference. Guide contribution A walkthrough, patch, test, component, or verification result maintained with this guide, not an official release or endorsement.

The walkthroughs label these handoffs at the steps where they happen. Keep the original notices with code and assets you reuse. A physical check in one app does not certify another app, device or image.

docs.title: Keep an honest progress record
docs.text:
Use separate milestones: source builds; desktop behavior checked; arm64 package built and inspected; installed app checked; physical input/peripherals checked; release reviewed. Mark unperformed checks pending, with the reason. A stationary GPS or Wi-Fi check, for example, cannot prove performance while walking a survey.

The independent-reader check is a short handoff for someone trying this guide without the original chat history. Their experience will tell me which instructions still need work.

docs.title: Store readiness checklist
docs.text: Use this alongside chapters 6 and 8. Reviewed 2026-11-23 against packages b6c559a and AppBuilder 042356c, plus the official submission guide. Check for upstream changes again before publishing; this dated snapshot does not reserve a code/name or guarantee future Store approval.

docs.title: Listing and package
docs.text:
• [ ] Package name, display title, actual binary/runtime version and manifest agree.
  • [ ] Unique title (case/whitespace normalized) and four-letter/digit share code (case-insensitive); check current catalog and reserved/taken-down names.
  • [ ] One or two exact allowed categories; accurate summary/description, prerequisites, author, source URL and license. Remove inherited template identities.
  • [ ] Exactly seven boolean permission declarations, including supervisor behavior.
  • [ ] One to six 320×170 PNG screenshots and a square 128–512 PNG Store icon; inspect their actual contents/metadata for sensitive information.
  • [ ] Inspect actual .deb: architecture, Maintainer, Debian version/revision, launcher entry/icon/Exec, package-related paths/names, dependency metadata, service identities, modes, udev rules and maintainer-script text.
  • [ ] No prohibited root/default-user system services, setuid/setgid files, device nodes, unrelated system paths or dangerous installer patterns.
  • [ ] Dependency plan records bundled components, Debian dependencies, external prerequisites, supported versions/ABI and ongoing updates/license obligations.
  • [ ] Run preflight on the exact release candidate; resolve all local blockers and review warnings. Save its JSON privately with evidence.

docs.title: Quality, safety and evidence
docs.text:
• [ ] Fresh supported image: dependencies install, app opens from the launcher, missing/incompatible prerequisites produce useful recovery instructions.
  • [ ] Actual upgrade preserves user settings/data, restarts changed services, and verifies live version/PID/privilege state. Test cold boot and uninstall.
  • [ ] Applicable keyboard/camera/radio/GPS/network checks have explicit outcomes; record simulator/container/replay/physical checks separately and state gaps.
  • [ ] Secrets/sensitivity review covers code, history, package, images, logs and video. License notices/source obligations reviewed for bundled components.
  • [ ] Public source commit/tag, exact artifact SHA-256 and test results recorded. Verify downloads again after publication; do not substitute a rebuild.
  • [ ] Synthetic hardware-demo content prepared; no account tokens, messages, real coordinates, private channel QR/URL or unnecessary device identifiers.

docs.title: Submission and later updates
docs.text:
1. Review first. The checklist/preflight does not log in or submit. Resolve open policy questions and select the concrete artifact/listing/video first.
  2. Choose a submission route and authenticate only for publishing. The official Developer Center also accepts a .deb, parses its metadata and creates the submission PR after the contributor confirms upload. It and the CLI share server-side policy; neither is a way around review. For the CLI, czdev login uses GitHub device flow and stores credentials locally. Protect those credentials and use the intended account: the recorded uploader controls the package name. It is not based on matching the Debian Maintainer's email.
  3. Publish deliberately. czdev publish --deb <exact-file> uploads the binary to a release in the contributor's packages fork and opens a metadata/manifest PR against CardputerZero/packages. This is a write operation. There is no publish --dry-run in the reviewed CLI. On acceptance, the official pipeline promotes the binary and regenerates the catalog/index.
  4. First submission. Post a short video of the app running on a real CardputerZero in the PR comments; a maintainer reviews/merges it. Passing CI does not auto-merge a new package name. Track PR approval, promotion/index job success and the final listing/download independently.
  5. Binary updates. The current catalog retains the highest Debian version per app; promotion can supersede older manifests and later clean their official binary assets. Do not promise users a permanent Store rollback archive; keep a separate verified release/rollback plan. Use the recorded owning account and a strictly higher Debian version. The reviewed policy allows validated updates to merge automatically; versioning is not determined by the GitHub release title/tag. 1.0.0~rc1-1 sorts before 1.0.0-1; marking a GitHub release “prerelease” does not change an embedded Debian Version: 1.0.0-1. Decide version policy before a candidate is submitted and never replace an accepted version's bytes.
  6. Listing-only updates. czdev publish --meta-only updates an existing listing without a new binary/version, subject to ownership and metadata checks. Retain assigned identity (uuid, existing share code) and verify staged assets.

References: schema/review rules, publishing implementation, validation, first-release/automatic-update merge gate.

docs.title: Worked example: correcting an overconfident submission report
docs.text:
The supplied Mesh submission report was checked against source and the real 0.1.8 CI artifact, rather than accepted as proof of readiness. These corrections are useful for any app:

Report item Verified disposition and lesson Empty share code / categories Communication, Utilities Real manifest blockers; use an available code and exact enum values. Availability is not a reservation “Only two items remain; the package already satisfies the gate” Incorrect. Local preflight also rejects the 100×100 Store icon, /usr/bin/mesh-launch name, and /usr/lib/systemd/user/cardputerzero-mesh-supervisor.service path Non-root firewall account and a user supervisor mean the package passes These address service identity; path and other policies still apply. Resolve the legitimate user-unit path conflict without weakening security A debian-arm64.yml workflow builds every package Mesh actually uses the debian-arm64 job in .github/workflows/regressions.yml; link the real workflow and its successful run Example uses 0.1.7 Current reviewed candidate is 0.1.8, Debian 0.1.8-rev1; use metadata from the selected artifact, not copied version examples Separate installation of meshtasticd/Python dependencies is always correct Historical Mesh versions chose separate prerequisites; 0.1.19 uses a maintained private bundle plus Debian OS dependencies. Evaluate the current version and test first-run/upgrade/removal; do not copy an old plan blindly docs/ does not ship Mesh installs Markdown/images under /usr/share/doc/cardputerzero-mesh/docs, excluding generated PDFs; inspect install rules/archive, not assumptions

Evidence: Mesh source fab958d, package SHA-256 8ff56073d45b43ed1cd1212f46bbdfcc9e345219c0897fbdf97d5fac2ad7b3b4; historical policy/catalog revision 94eb8d7 reviewed on 2026-11-16. A filename-normalization warning also notes that czdev uploads cardputerzero-mesh_0.1.8-rev1_arm64.deb based on the control fields. Missing localization is advisory. No Store submission was performed in this guide pass, and these blockers are not described as repaired in the installed app. This record is a dated example, not current app status.

docs.title: Current-review boundaries
docs.text:
Both official policy-script hashes are unchanged from the previous lock; the catalog, CLI and publishing lifecycle have advanced. The lock/CI checkout is updated only after comparing those sources. Run the exact candidate against this current catalog: a previously available title/code can become occupied. On this snapshot MESH belongs to meshtandem; an older Mesh preflight pass is not a reservation. See the application's dated submission-readiness report.

Official preinstalled apps and third-party Store packages can have different privilege policies. The official GPS example's root/sudo packaging is not a third-party exemption from the Store's no-root rule. Reuse its appropriate parser/model ideas while preserving least privilege in the package being submitted.

docs.title: Personal UI preferences
docs.text: Decisions are recorded component by component. A locked preference is the default for my own apps; revisit any necessary app-specific exception explicitly. Preserve the official shell/input/backend boundaries. This record does not implement a library or change existing apps.

docs.title: Locked: home menu — exact Mesh carousel
docs.text:
Agreed 2026-11-18. The owner wants the home carousel exactly as designed in Mesh, including its look and feel. Mesh's actual implementation is the authoritative reference; the illustrative comparison is not a pixel/font/motion specification.

Reference: m5stack-cardputer-zero-mesh-app, commit 5f21eebe83402119c5c3ad3a3aee3aef905fccd3, principally src/view/screens/menu_screen.cpp. Supporting file hashes are in the reference manifest.

  • Large centered icon above its label; faint previous/next icons at the edges.
  • Current geometry: 40 px center icon font, 28 px neighbor icon font, 40% neighbor opacity, 12 px edge offsets and 10 px icon/label gap. Label uses the existing 17 px regular standard-font path with the existing 18 px fallback.
  • Directional slide and simultaneous fade over 180 ms, with a 46 px slide and the current ease-out slide path. Preserve correct direction through wraparound.
  • Left/right selection, wrapping and Enter activation; retain the existing keyboard routing and selected-item state. Theme changes recolor without triggering selection animation; initial display does not animate in.
  • Preserve the actual light/dark home appearance, including Mesh's current primary/disabled colors and surface treatment. A global palette decision for other components is still open; do not silently substitute the comparison's palette for this exact reference.
  • Preserve the reference home geometry: 320×170, 30 px title region and content below it. The position indicator in the next section is the agreed addition. The home implementation has no added bottom function-key lane; do not import the illustrative preview's footer as an approved preference.

App-specific destinations, labels and appropriate icon glyphs can represent the new app's own functions. That is content substitution, not permission to redesign the carousel. Preserve attribution and the selected official foundation's lifecycle/focus ownership when later implementing reuse.

docs.title: Locked: home-carousel position indicator
docs.text:
Agreed 2026-11-26. Keep the Mesh home carousel geometry and directional animation, and add the NFC Tools position bar below the home label. Center the row, use NFC Tools’ vertical spacing (menu title top y=82, dot row y=138 on 320×170), and use a wider accent pill for the current slot and small muted dots for the others, and update it with the carousel selection, including wrap. Do not animate or add a footer for the indicator. This is distinct from the right-edge overflow bar used on a submenu list. The reusable LVGL component and its source notes live with the guide.

Keep the top-bar battery percentage plain text and right-aligned when available. No battery glyph and no fabricated percentage if the device does not report one.

docs.title: Locked: submenu-list selection and navigation cues
docs.text:
Confirmed 2026-11-18: use Mesh's rounded selected row, subtle background fill and colored stripe on the left. Reference: the same Mesh commit above, src/view/widgets/list_selection.h, style_list_row() / select_list_row(). The existing implementation uses a 6 px radius, palette button fill and 3 px left border in the primary color; changing selection clears the old row's selection styling and scrolls the newly selected row into view. Screens retain their own item identity and navigation state.

Additional rules supplied by the owner on 2026-11-18:

  • If the highlighted entry opens a submenu, show a right-facing chevron (>) at the right of the row. Do not use it as a generic decoration on every row.
  • If content extends beyond the visible screen, show a slim bar on the right with a moving position marker, so the user can see that more content exists. Keep it available as navigation reveals items above/below; omit it when all content fits. Reserve space so it does not obscure labels or chevrons.
  • Use Up and Down for vertical selection (Fn+F/Fn+X on Cardputer Zero; bare F/X may be contextual aliases outside editors). Left and Right move the home carousel or adjust a focused value, never select a vertical row.
  • Use wrap-around list navigation: Down from the last selectable entry moves to the first; Up from the first moves to the last. Scroll the visible list to keep the new selection in view, including after wrapping. Moving selection does not activate/open the entry.
  • The position bar is conditional on actual content exceeding the visible list area, not merely on the list being nonempty. Wrapping updates its marker to the new position. An empty list has no selection; a single selectable item remains selected. Preserve this behavior if item count or row height changes.
  • Visual reference for that bar: NFC Tools' Settings main page, inspected in build/amber/settings.png and src/ui/app.cpp::App::list. The example shows three of five rows, a thin right-side track and an accent-colored marker.

The NFC source/render reference is recorded by hash in the manifest and comes from an uncommitted working tree, not its HEAD alone. Its current list renderer draws the bar for every nonempty list and draws chevrons on all displayed rows. Those existing conditions are not the owner's specified rules; reuse the visual reference while implementing the conditional behaviors above in any later work. No NFC change is made here. Typography and row content are not locked by these cues.

The owner's wrap-around request is recorded as component behavior during this preference walkthrough. No reusable list implementation exists from this record, and this update does not claim it has been applied to an existing app.

docs.title: Locked: On/Off setting rows
docs.text:
Agreed 2026-11-18: display the setting's On or Off value as text on the right, with its name on the left. Use this instead of a drawn toggle switch or checkmark for ordinary boolean settings. A row that changes a value inline does not receive a submenu chevron; reserve > for submenu navigation.

Example: Save history on the left and On on the right. The value must reflect the setting's known state; handling pending/unknown states and any necessary confirmation remains part of the app's behavior contract, not a reason to display a false On/Off value. This preference selects presentation, not new toggle or confirmation behavior.

docs.title: Locked: direct choices and task forms
docs.text:
Agreed 2026-11-22: a setting with two choices changes directly on its row; Appearance alternates Light/Dark without a submenu. More than two choices open an appropriate selection menu with the current value selected. Inline actions do not receive a submenu chevron. Preserve any specific consent required for privacy, transmission or irreversible effects; do not show an unconfirmed value as already applied.

Group everything needed for a task in one place. A channel setup form includes its related channel, radio, sharing and save fields rather than requiring trips through Settings. Use visible groups inside the same form, identify changes that affect the whole radio, preserve edits on errors, and keep Save reachable while scrolling. The form itself is the review; do not add a generic second review page. Specific consequential changes can require targeted acknowledgment.

Use readable contrast for important values and results in both themes, plain language for outcomes, non-color cues where color carries meaning, and Cancel-first confirmation for irreversible deletion when Undo is unavailable. These are my interaction preferences; they do not create a replacement shell or a universal requirement for every project. Source and physical qualification remain app-specific. Mesh's 0.1.15 candidate implements a focused refinement; its verification record owns the actual results and remaining checks.

docs.title: Locked: header battery presentation
docs.text: Agreed 2026-11-23: omit the battery icon from the app header. Mesh retains the numeric charge percentage when battery data is available, with no substitute charging/battery glyph. This is my presentation preference, not a platform requirement or a replacement for the official shell/status source. Preserve truthful unknown/absent state and existing backend ownership. Do not add polling or change telemetry merely to remove a decorative icon. Other apps are not silently migrated by this documentation update.

docs.text:

  • Body/supporting typography and spacing outside the locked home reference.
  • Overall palette policy and app-specific accent choices.
  • Status/title bars and footer actions outside this home reference.
  • Editors/forms, Help, confirmations, notifications and progress.

No implementation, extraction, new timing measurement, device test or global restyling is claimed by this decision record.

docs.title: Worked example: Mesh and the lessons it contributed
docs.text: Mesh is one application built with a native LVGL UI and a Python radio service. Its channels, acknowledgments, private-channel keys and persistence policy explain many of this guide's original examples. They are optional application concerns. A calculator or local notes app does not need the radio service or its firewall.

docs.title: Current dependency distribution (0.1.19)
docs.text:
The older source/evidence examples below retain their recorded versions. Mesh 0.1.19 now bundles the GPS-corrected native radio and 15 locked Python wheels in one installer, with Debian supplying standard OS libraries. The existing user service prepares its private environment offline; a separate global daemon and manual user pip setup are no longer required. This changes distribution, not the UI/supervisor ownership boundary or the official components it reuses.

Qualified package/device evidence identifies exact source/bytes and separates minimal Debian tests from the owner-deferred fresh-image hardware test. The current install/backup/recovery runbook and build/source instructions are maintained operational guidance, not immutable historical evidence.

docs.title: Evidence and scope
docs.text:
The preserved sections below come from the previous guide revision, reviewed 2026-11-16. Their detailed wording is retained to avoid losing the failures that motivated the general rules. Read them as Mesh-specific examples, alongside architecture choices, project sections and the lesson index.

Implementation and evidence are in the pinned Mesh source, remediation record, keyboard checks and maintenance measurements. The candidate has 98 backend tests plus native and package checks. Those results qualify that application/revision, not every future app or all official services. Outdoor GPS, live public-peer interoperability and physical IPv6 qualification remain separate gaps; simulated events do not constitute a physical all-key sweep. No new device qualification is claimed by reorganizing this guide.

docs.title: Subsequent modularity and input maintenance
docs.text: Mesh 0.1.11 adds bounded input polling and source-owned hold cleanup. The architecture decision explains its purpose, benefits, costs and official-platform compatibility. The M5Stack review package keeps this maintenance separate from the optional Template integration. The original lesson blocks below remain preserved at their stated source revision.

docs.title: Subsequent GPS integration qualification
docs.text: The 2026-11-23 GPS record supersedes the earlier outdoor-GPS gap for that fitted receiver and exact versions. App 0.1.17 refreshes exported local-node snapshots without enabling location broadcasts. A separate pinned Meshtastic native-service patch extends its ATGM identification window from 500 to 1500ms after seven of eight measured replies arrived later than 500ms. The driver had suppressed normal output before probing. That is a measured third-party integration problem, not an official GPS-app defect. Its reserved nonce, 30s snapshot interval and two-minute freshness policy are Mesh-specific, not defaults for other GPS apps. The general GPS section explains the transferable cache, ownership, privacy, timing and qualification lessons.

docs.title: Subsequent everyday-use refinement
docs.text:
Mesh 0.1.15's implementation and qualification record provide later evidence for readable editor states, stable Cancel-first deletion, grouped forms, explicit saved-setup consequences and English case-insensitive search. The installed candidate passed its native/backend/package gates, ordinary-user synthetic device replay and the owner's specified physical checks. Those checks did not add powered-radio, public-peer or outdoor GPS qualification.

The upgrade also demonstrated why files and running processes must be checked separately: the existing service still reported the old version until restarted through its normal lifecycle. A GUI version-query attempt opened a UI because that option was unsupported; the temporary instance was stopped. The general build/install guidance records safer verification and preservation checks. These results qualify the named Mesh revision, not a reusable library or another application's hardware.

docs.title: Make the boundary authoritative
docs.text:
The UI may show a local message echo, but the supervisor must retain its actual status. Store ACK/NAK results before broadcasting; a reconnect snapshot must not turn Delivered back into Sending. Retries need a stable message ID plus a new attempt token so an old ACK cannot complete the new attempt. Apply retention to existing history immediately, broadcast removals, and bound total history even when a user chooses “All.” Reapply persisted client preferences on reconnect and define which client wins if multiple clients choose different policies.

Every asynchronous result needs identity: a request ID plus the target channel, node or record ID. Indexing a refreshed vector is unsafe across callbacks. Capture stable IDs, resolve them again before acting, and cancel acceptance when a user dismisses the pending overlay. This applies especially to secret-bearing results such as share codes: a hardcoded group name can disclose another group's key.

docs.title: Preserve identity and durable intent safely
docs.text:
A slot or vector index is a location, not an identity. When configuration can replace its contents, bind conversations, drafts, selections, retries and commands to a stable identity and validate it at the owner before acting. For secret-bearing configurations, use a keyed local digest rather than exposing the secret or a brute-forceable plain hash. Moving the same logical record can preserve identity; changing its key/name should archive old context instead of silently rerouting it.

Keep bounded durable history authoritative in the supervisor. Commit ACK/failure, retention and deletion changes before publishing snapshots. Persist drafts without turning them into a replay queue. An interrupted send should become Failed after restart, with an honest uncertainty reason. Distinguish acceptance by an API, a mesh acknowledgment, a recipient acknowledgment and a read receipt; never infer a later stage from an earlier one. Confirm the acknowledgment source before naming a recipient.

If opting out of disk history retains an active RAM session, define what opting back in saves. Persist its existing drafts without requiring another keystroke; test an immediate restart after the preference change and notify every client.

For related preference files, record and sync a complete validated transaction, then roll it forward idempotently after interruption. Applying a saved hardware profile must not restore transmission or privacy consent as a side effect.

Exercise the real event library when testing callback registration. A child topic can inherit required arguments from its parent; changing one listener's optional parameters can make another subscription fail during startup. Register the same parent/child listeners as production and deliver representative events. Count remote RF reception from received packets, rather than local admin replies or cached node-update notifications.

Audit greeting builders as part of the live control path. Send one bounded history snapshot, avoid redundant client requests, and perform slow dependency probes outside lifecycle locks. Cache informational version queries while forcing a fresh compatibility check before hardware starts. Fresh security verdicts need their own age policy. Capture shared interface references and guard every library dereference when constructing status, even if most callers already hold a lock.

docs.title: Privacy state and asynchronous overlays
docs.text:
Render device settings as confirmed values, Pending, or Unknown. Do not optimistically flip a privacy boolean before the supervisor/device confirms it; an offline “Off” can mislead someone carrying a radio. Use request IDs and a deadline, and expire pending state if the response never arrives. Configuration cache writes are not readback. Make the target explicit when enabling behavior on one channel/group.

An overlay awaiting a result must stop accepting that result after Esc, navigation or teardown. Match the response to both request and target. Use stable record IDs across list rebuilds, never pointers into a vector that can reallocate. Tie LVGL observers to an object's lifetime or explicitly remove them. Regression-test list reordering while details or an action menu is open.

Apply deadlines to every waiting view, including generic service operations. Timeout or disconnect means the result may be unknown; do not claim a write was rolled back. Clear request acceptance on dismissal, echo valid IDs on validation errors, and ignore repeated Return while busy. Keep request correlation fields separate from the object being changed (for example, request id and target message_id).

docs.title: First run and uncertain live data
docs.text:
A complete first run needs a safe default, a reviewable configuration, dependency failure messages, and a separate deliberate step to enable hardware transmission. Never overwrite an existing profile to make the wizard succeed. Show receive-only separately from disconnected and transmitting states. Surface the actual stop reason in diagnostics instead of hiding every failure behind a generic Error.

Treat GPS data as a measurement with a timestamp. Validate finite coordinates, bounds, clock plausibility and freshness at the owner, even if the UI displays a marker. Coalesce telemetry updates and refresh age labels; a cached location must not look like a new fix. Debounce draft persistence to avoid a disk transaction on every keystroke, flush on navigation, and keep rejected sends editable. Quiet hours need explicit local-time semantics and a window that works across midnight.

Keep a conversation registry independent of messages. Draft-only, pinned and cleared conversations must remain reachable after rebuilding the list; deleting the conversation must remove that saved state too. Bind a DM draft to both peer and selected channel, so a channel change cannot move unsent text to another mesh.

Distinguish enabling the GPS receiver from consenting to location broadcasts. A timestamp without valid coordinates is not a fix. Show stale/unknown locations as last known, and test an actual clear-sky fix separately from parser validation.

Test the actual camera stack. A CSI sensor's /dev/video0 may be a raw sensor/ISP node, not a webcam stream. On the stock image, use a fixed libcamera/rpicam capture command with bounded dimensions/time and decode in memory; do not save private camera frames merely to test a scanner. Missing decoder libraries and camera-busy failures should produce actionable UI errors, not a misleading "no QR found." Measure capture startup on the device before choosing the deadline; include startup, exposure and decoding within a bounded total budget.

Give a camera operation a ready state with an explicit keyboard action such as Return: scan. Publish a visible busy state before dispatching asynchronous work, ignore repeated Return while busy, and show success or an actionable retry after the matching result. Correlate replies by request ID; dismissed or superseded results and unsolicited state updates must not replace a newer view. Clear cached results when starting a new request. On disconnect, explain that the result is unknown if the operation could already have changed state. If Escape only leaves the view, say so; do not imply that it cancels hardware work or rolls back an import. Keep simulator limitations in development docs instead of user prompts.

When scanning can lead to configuration changes, separate capture, preview and commit. Keep the decoded secret on the backend, return a nonsecret preview, and require a Cancel-first confirmation. Bind its short-lived token to the requesting connection and the exact configuration shown. Changing configuration, Escape or teardown must invalidate the preview, including work still queued on the server. Give one bounded camera job a cancellation event and own its helper/child process group. Keep capture off the serialized radio worker; commit radio writes there only after confirmation. Announce committed results if their view has been left.

Measure queue pressure with the actual debounce semantics. A 650 ms typing-pause debounce is different from a periodic write every 650 ms. Local draft/history commits should not wait behind camera/admin work: serialize local state with its own lock while preserving explicit persistence-barrier ordering. Test that local writes and radio status still progress while the slow operation is blocked.

Compare effective state before rebuilding LVGL object trees. A draft echo can be identical to the local value; merge pending local edits first and still process request completion even when no redraw is needed. Genuine pin, deletion and history-preference changes must continue to notify observers. When a list is rebuilt, preserve its highlighted identity through reordering and define a stable tie order. Prepare typed rows with one indexed pass before rendering; search the history once instead of once per conversation.

docs.title: Keep context and keyboard help readable
docs.text:
On a 320x170 screen, keep the active channel/target in a fixed conversation header and reserve the footer for short keyboard hints or compose input. Bound long names and preserve the routing identity and privacy label before truncating the less critical text. Check actual pixel bounds with the real fonts, including long peer names, message selection, composing, scrolling and returning to the list.

Render selection lines in both themes. An LVGL outline sits outside an object's bounds and can be clipped by a tightly fitted parent. Use an inside border or reserve clearance through the parent chain so the entire line stays visible. When adding a border, account for its width in the content inset; keep the sum of border and padding stable so selection does not move the text or resize the row.

Give settings stable action keys independent of display order. Group related options with nonselectable headings; navigation should visit actual settings only. Tests should find the selected label rather than blindly pressing Down a historic number of times, especially before transmission or privacy actions. Long information overlays need keyboard scrolling as well as an Escape path.

docs.title: Radio route validation
docs.text: • Validate every route to an RF action. A DM destination does not bypass channel validation. Reject broadcast aliases disguised as destinations. Check real key formats and public/private classification, not just a channel name. Supporting public channels is compatible with a secure client: use clear labels, explicit selection, and separate location opt-in. Enabling location on one channel must not also enable another. Preserve channel identity through pickers, details, intents and share replies.

docs.title: Licensing choices in this application
docs.text:
• Mind the copyleft. The Meshtastic stack (meshtasticd, the meshtastic Python library) is GPL-3.0. If any of your code links a GPL library in-process, that code must be GPL-compatible. A clean, real-world split:
  • Your C++/LVGL UI stays MIT — it only talks to the other process over a socket (separate program; preserve the distinct licenses and interfaces).
  • The supervisor incorporates the GPL client library and is licensed GPL-3.0-or-later.
  • 0.1.19 bundles the qualified daemon and client wheels, with original notices and paired corresponding source. Earlier examples used separate prerequisites. Neither arrangement is mandatory for other apps; the right plan depends on supported images, maintenance and user installation needs. See the dependency plans.
  • Running a separate GPL program as a subprocess (e.g. launching meshtasticd) does not by itself determine the other program's license; the nature of the integration and applicable terms still matter. The example publishes both components as open source with explicit licenses.

docs.title: Choose the project sections you need
docs.text:
First app? Take the short route before choosing extras.

All apps use the common foundation. Add the sections below only when their capabilities apply. A topic being documented does not mean it is implemented or qualified in every example application.

Project type Additional guidance Evidence status Calculator, notes, timer, simple game Local utilities Architecture/acceptance recipe; no new device app claimed Text, drafts, searchable records, messaging Persistence and messaging General rules with detailed Mesh examples; transports differ GPS receiver or maps GPS and maps Official GPS reuse plus cache/ownership/privacy/startup qualification; fitted Mesh test passed, other sources need their own evidence Camera or QR scanner Camera and QR Mesh CSI capture experience; qualify the actual sensor/image/decoder NFC, GPIO/I2C/SPI or another Cap Hardware ownership Conditional safety/lifecycle recipe; verify each peripheral's documentation LoRa Cap Radio bring-up plus hardware ownership Board/Cap-specific wiring and lessons; not a universal pinout Network client/server or remote control Networking Threat-model/acceptance recipe; private local daemons and remote services differ Audio, recording or media playback Audio and media Integration recipe and official examples; not qualified by Mesh tests

For any new hardware capability, first identify the board/image/peripheral, permissions, safe acquisition/release sequence and unsupported behavior. Use a fake implementation for UI tests. Add real-device acceptance checks separately. Do not copy a Mesh-only channel, key or daemon dependency into an unrelated app.

Guide index · Preserved lessons

docs.title: Audio, recording and media playback
docs.text: Start with the intended device image's ordinary user-session audio facilities or a compatible official media service. Inspect the official Music and Recorder apps as references, not as proof that every backend, image or recording format has been tested here. A privileged process may not inherit access to the user's audio session; avoid privilege escalation as an audio-routing workaround.

docs.title: App behavior
docs.text:
Keep decoding/capture off the UI thread, bound buffers and define pause/stop/close semantics. Own workers and device handles through cancellation and failure. Make recording visible, require deliberate activation, choose a private destination and explain retention/deletion. Permission failure, busy device, unsupported codec and storage-full errors should produce different actionable messages.

Budget waveform/album-art assets and redraw work for the small display/memory. Define which controls need physical press/release/repeat semantics instead of text or generic navigation. Keep playback/recording state confirmed by its owner.

docs.title: Acceptance checks
docs.text:
Test synthetic media, malformed/truncated content, no output/input device, concurrent ownership, cancellation, full storage and restart. Qualify speaker/microphone, latency, clipping, route changes and long-running resource use on the intended image. Those are proposed acceptance checks, not results established by Mesh.

Project selector

docs.title: Camera capture and QR scanning
docs.text: Inspect the camera stack on the target image. A CSI sensor's /dev/video0 can be a sensor/ISP node rather than a ready webcam stream. Mesh uses a fixed libcamera/rpicam capture with bounded dimensions/time and in-memory decoding; other apps may use a compatible official camera service. Check the actual backend, permissions and runtime dependencies before choosing either path.

docs.title: Visible operation and ownership
docs.text:
Show Ready with an explicit keyboard action, publish Scanning/Busy before work starts, ignore repeated starts and return an actionable result or retry. Correlate results by request and target. Clear stale results before a new operation and stop accepting late replies after dismissal. Explain whether Escape cancels work or merely leaves the view; it does not automatically roll back a committed action.

Bound capture plus exposure/startup plus decode within a measured total deadline. Give the owner a cancellation mechanism and control its helper/process group. Camera-busy and missing-decoder failures are not equivalent to "no QR found". Keep unrelated local saves and status updates responsive while capture is blocked.

docs.title: QR codes that change configuration
docs.text: Decoded text is untrusted. Validate format, length, destination and permitted action. For a secret/configuration import, separate capture, nonsecret preview and explicit commit. Keep the secret at its owner; bind short-lived preview authorization to the requesting session and exact reviewed configuration. Invalidate it on cancellation, configuration change or teardown, including queued work. Announce actual commits when their original view has gone away. These rules apply beyond radio channels.

docs.title: Acceptance checks
docs.text:
Test synthetic codes, malformed/oversized content, missing/busy camera, timeout, repeated Return, cancellation and late/wrong-target replies. Qualify the actual camera in good light and realistic distances on the supported image. Do not retain private camera frames just for diagnostics or ship usable private QR codes in tests. See the preserved Mesh camera/import lessons.

Project selector

docs.title: GPS receivers and maps
docs.text: This section helps any CardputerZero app consume GPS reliably: a map, survey logger, tracker or local instrument. It complements the official hardware and app guidance. It does not introduce a GPS framework, require Mesh's supervisor, or replace M5Stack's receiver support. USB receiver work remains unqualified in my apps; the source-selection guidance below is a design checklist.

docs.title: Start with what M5Stack already provides
docs.text:
Reviewed 2026-11-23. Use the official Zero usage guide for the built-in GPS app and Cap specification for wiring, supply, UART, antenna and power-off-before-removal precautions. Do not substitute ESP32 Cardputer/ADV GPIO examples for Zero's Linux device paths. For this fitted receiver, GNSS is on the Cap; it is not evidence of GPS in a bare Zero.

The official GPS app already offers useful implementation patterns:

Official source What to reuse or evaluate src/gps/linux_serial_backend.cpp Console conflict check, nonblocking reads, advisory lock plus exclusive-open request, restoration and cleanup src/gps/nmea_decoder.cpp Bounded sentence assembly/checksum handling and per-field validity src/models/gps_model.cpp, tests/gps_model_test.cpp Separate data/fix ages, no-data/search/fix/stale/error states, bounded work and retry tests src/views/details_panel.cpp Receiver/data diagnostics instead of an unexplained empty map

Decision: reuse or adapt the official direct-receiver model when it fits. When another service owns the receiver, consume that service's supported API; do not start a second raw reader just to reuse a serial example. Keep the app's chosen official shell, lifecycle and resource contracts.

The official GPS README describes root/sudo packaging for its preinstalled power-control path. That is not a third-party Store exemption: the current development rules prohibit apps running as root. Adapt privilege/resource integration rather than copying that packaging into a Store app. See hardware ownership.

docs.title: What my experience adds
docs.text: The reviewed official usage/specification pages explain hardware and operation; the source already covers many parser, age and ownership concerns. The following is additional application-integration and qualification guidance, not a claim that these topics are absent from every M5Stack document or that its GPS app is broken. Reviewed sources/hashes are in the evidence record.

docs.title: Prove each layer separately
docs.text:
A working receiver does not prove a working application. Follow the actual path:

Receiver -> resource owner -> exported API -> client cache -> UI/map.

Layer Evidence to seek Receiver Recent valid fixes from the receiver; counts/checksums can prove activity without saving coordinates Resource owner The owning process has accepted the fix and has the correct power/port/profile API The supported response really exports the current fix and the fields the app needs Client A cache receives newer measurements, including loss-of-fix, after connect/reconnect UI The actual screen shows the fix, its source and truthful age/last-known state

If raw fixes exist but a map is empty, investigate the boundaries above before changing receiver firmware, baud rate, antenna or sharing settings. A client method named “get current position” may only return a cache. Repeated reads of that cache cannot produce an update that the service never exported.

Use documented stream/snapshot support. Bound refresh frequency, outstanding requests, completion deadlines and retry backoff. Correlate replies with the current connection/source generation so an old reply cannot update a replacement receiver. Do not clear unrelated client state or open a competing connection to force a refresh. Neither a successful API reply nor new bytes proves a new fix.

docs.title: Preserve measurement time and missing fields
docs.text:
Represent validity, acquisition time/age and source explicitly. Keep transport receipt time separate: receiving the same cached fix again must not reset its age. Use a local monotonic clock for elapsed deadlines; handle source UTC changes, unknown time and implausible future timestamps separately. A monotonic timestamp from another boot/device is not directly comparable to your current clock.

Choose stale thresholds for the receiver cadence, transport delay and action's risk. The official live viewer uses a different age policy from Mesh's cached map; neither value is a universal GPS rule. A valid old position may be shown as last known, while navigation, geofence actions or sending may need a fresh fix. Do not silently repeat an old location as a new measurement.

Validate finite coordinates and geographic bounds. Missing coordinates should be explicit, not invented at (0, 0); that coordinate is itself a real place and needs a validity flag to interpret correctly. Distinguish satellites visible, satellites used and a valid fix. An API that omits satellite count should show unknown, not zero or a count copied from a different diagnostic/source. Expose altitude, quality/accuracy and constellation details only when supported.

docs.title: Treat startup commands as state changes
docs.text:
Identify the exact receiver, owner/library version and protocol before choosing a workaround. An apparently simple discovery routine may first suppress normal output. A too-short identification timeout can then leave an enabled receiver silent. Measure repeated reply latency and command side effects, including the receiver's output schedule, before changing a deadline.

Separate power/port initialization, model identification and satellite acquisition timeouts. Increasing one is not a cure for another. Every wait still needs a bound, cancellation and useful retry/error state. Check whether an attempt changed receiver output and how normal operation is recovered. Do not hide failures with endless reset loops, silently flash firmware or persistently change baud/rate/ constellation settings as an unproven repair.

docs.title: Keep diagnostics exclusive and location private
docs.text:
There should be one physical resource owner. Access through its API during normal operation. For a raw diagnostic, stop that owner normally, acquire the supported hardware/port lease, run a bounded reader, then restore the prior settings and owner. The official lock/exclusive-open pattern is useful, but do not assume unrelated programs all cooperate with an advisory lock. Never launch a separate GPS viewer while a radio service owns the same UART.

Receiver enablement is separate from permission to record, transmit or upload location. A local map must work with sharing Off. Check this explicitly. A Cap may share power/resources with other hardware, so retain its documented safety requirements even when the app only wants GPS; do not generalize a rail or pinout to other receivers.

For support logs, prefer fix booleans, age, model, error category, latency and sentence/checksum counts. Raw NMEA, coordinates, track files, screenshots and USB serial identities can reveal a home or route. Redact or omit them from public issues and videos; obtain permission before any purposeful location export.

docs.title: Choosing internal or external sources
docs.text:
Specify source selection before implementing USB support: manual selection or a stated priority; what happens on unplug; when fallback is allowed; how stale fixes are labeled; and whether the user's choice survives restart. Show the active source. Reconnecting a new receiver must not relabel the previous receiver's cached position as its fresh fix.

Use supported discovery/stable identity where available, not an assumption that /dev/ttyUSB0 always names the same device. Check driver/interface, permissions, protocol, speed and power needs. Keep identifying serial numbers private. An external antenna is not automatically a new GPS receiver. USB switching can also remove the maintenance connection; plan network access independently.

These are design requirements, not a claim that the deferred USB dongle is supported, automatically preferred, or physically tested.

docs.title: Acceptance checks
docs.text:
1. Test synthetic valid, invalid, absent, stale, future, malformed and out-of-range measurements, including per-field omissions and repeated cached fixes.
  2. Test partial/oversized/bad-checksum input through the selected parser when consuming raw data. Reuse official tests/components where suitable.
  3. Test receiver enable/disable independently of sharing. Check one resource owner and no location emission when sharing is Off.
  4. Exercise API timeout, reconnect, late replies, source replacement and clock changes. Confirm no fabricated freshness or loss of unrelated app state.
  5. Use the actual intended receiver outdoors with a clear sky view and safe hardware setup. First acquisition time depends on conditions; a five-minute timeout alone does not prove defective hardware.
  6. Observe successive acquisition timestamps across a steady interval, not just one coordinate. Check the real map/display and loss/stale/recovery states.
  7. Repeat starts and error/retry paths. Treat normal receiver restarts, a cold whole-device boot and long-term field use as different tests.
  8. Record exact app/dependency/package versions, elapsed time and reduced results. Preserve settings/data, restore intended operating mode and retain rollback.

Mesh's qualification record now includes actual raw receiver fixes, a local-cache correction, owner-confirmed Map marker, eight receiver starts and a final 31-sample/321.5-second outdoor watch. These bounded results supersede the old “outdoor unqualified” note here; they do not qualify every future app, a USB receiver or unlimited reliability.

The Mesh case study keeps its reserved API nonce, refresh interval and Meshtastic identification patch separate from this general recipe. Do not copy those settings into an unrelated receiver or call the Meshtastic defect an M5Stack firmware defect.

Project selector · Hardware ownership · LoRa-specific bring-up

docs.title: NFC, Caps and other hardware projects
docs.text: Use the documented interface for the exact board/peripheral revision. Determine whether an official compatible service already owns the resource. Record power, mux, GPIO/I2C/SPI/UART, permissions, shared-pin/rail conflicts and teardown before implementing acquisition. The LoRa sequence is specific to that Cap; it is not an NFC, audio or generic-GPIO recipe.

docs.title: Resource ownership and failure
docs.text:
Choose one owner and serialize conflicting operations. Acquire only necessary permissions and restore resources according to their safe order and prior state. Distinguish absent, busy, unsupported and failed initialization. Provide an appropriate retry/close path where useful, but do not claim that a presence dialog can verify an antenna or that every peripheral supports safe hot swapping.

If a process changes persistent power/mux state or starts child processes, design abrupt-death recovery. Stop/reap children before restoring shared hardware. Do not kill unrelated owners or reset system configuration to make a probe succeed. Test ordinary close, initialization failure and interruption with fake resources before device work.

docs.title: Acceptance checks
docs.text:
Check missing/busy hardware behavior and shared-resource transitions using the manufacturer's safe procedure. Verify permissions as the normal application user. Confirm actual hardware release after exit/failure and that another app can use it afterward. Disconnect/reconnect tests are appropriate only when the hardware supports them safely. Document qualification per board/image/peripheral, including power-cycle requirements; a UI simulator cannot qualify electrical behavior.

This section is development guidance for relevant projects. It does not add a Cap presence feature or change the current Mesh application's radio behavior.

Project selector

docs.title: Local utilities, notes and simple games
docs.text:
A calculator, timer or local notes tool can begin with one unprivileged process. Use the official shell, supported keyboard path and ordinary app settings. A backend process is optional. Keep file indexing or other slow work on bounded jobs and deliver results on the UI thread.

For a first build, use the official counter walkthrough. It reuses the existing demo rather than introducing a new utility framework.

docs.title: Decide the behavior before adding infrastructure
docs.text:
• Keep a calculator's state local; distinguish clear-entry, clear-all and Escape.
  • Use a monotonic clock for elapsed timers, and define whether they continue while the app is closed. A wall-clock change must not change an elapsed duration.
  • For notes, use stable record IDs and deliberate save/recovery behavior. Keep draft text on rejected saves; flush at defined close/navigation boundaries.
  • For games, distinguish text input from game key identity/repeat. Do not apply a navigation shortcut policy to every game key. Budget assets and redraw work.

docs.title: Acceptance checks
docs.text:
Exercise every action with the actual input adapter, long/empty text, repeated keys and overlays. Check focus and selection after deleting/reordering records. Test full-disk/save failures, restart and malformed settings if data persists. Measure memory/startup and timer behavior on the target; simulation alone does not prove frame rate, power use or hardware input.

The optional editor in the prepared keyboard proposal is a small integration example without a radio/service. It is not a completed notes application or evidence that a general library has two production consumers.

Project selector

docs.title: Persistent text, records and messaging
docs.text: The common UI rules cover responsive editing and stable selection. Add a durable record model when text must survive closing the app. A conversation/message model is needed only for a communications app.

docs.title: Persistence and identity
docs.text:
Use stable record IDs, bound total bytes/records and make the real state owner responsible for committed saves/deletions. Keep draft-only, pinned and cleared records reachable independently of received content. Do not use vector positions as identities across callbacks or configuration changes.

Define RAM-only versus disk history, what re-enabling storage saves, and deletion semantics. Metadata such as record/contact identifiers and pins can be sensitive even without message text. Test raw persisted rows after opt-out/restart. Private permissions are not encryption and logical deletion does not erase every flash, WAL or backup copy. See security.

docs.title: Transport-specific results
docs.text:
Define each transport stage honestly: queued, accepted by a local API, transmitted, acknowledged by a relay/recipient, failed or unknown. A transport ACK is not a read receipt. Match replies to a stable message and a particular attempt; ignore stale ACKs and validate their source. Preserve confirmed results through reconnects. Never automatically replay an uncertain or failed send after restart.

For Mesh, changing channel keys/names can change a routing identity. Archive the old context instead of silently sending its drafts to a replacement channel. A DM draft belongs to both its peer and selected channel. Those rules must be adapted explicitly for a different transport rather than inheriting LoRa fields.

docs.title: Search behavior
docs.text:
When search is offered, define which names, content and drafts it covers and how capitalization is handled. Test a match in an older saved item, a draft-only record, mixed capitalization and clearing the filter. Keep the search/display normalization separate from stored text and stable record IDs.

ASCII-only case matching is not full Unicode case folding. State that limit rather than claiming every language is handled; if broader matching is needed, choose an appropriate Unicode implementation and test accented text and supported scripts. Mesh 0.1.15 deliberately ignores English-letter capitalization while other characters still match exactly. Other applications should decide their own language requirements.

docs.title: Acceptance checks
docs.text:
Cover interrupted saves/sends, delayed and wrong-source replies, retries, reconnect snapshots, cap reductions, multiple clients and storage re-enable with existing RAM drafts followed by immediate restart. Check quiet hours across midnight only if notifications exist. Detailed Mesh lessons retain the concrete failure cases and acknowledgment distinctions.

Project selector

docs.title: Network clients and services
docs.text: First decide which peers may communicate and what they may do. A local private helper, a cloud API client and an intentionally remote server need different network policies. Do not impose Mesh's private-daemon firewall design on every app.

docs.title: Clients and background jobs
docs.text: Use authenticated encrypted connections where appropriate, validate certificates, bound messages/queues/time and keep retries cancellable. Store user credentials privately at runtime; never put them in examples, packages, logs or screenshots. Keep a reconnect from replaying a consequential action without an explicit policy. Document offline behavior and preserve recoverable edits on network failure.

docs.title: Private local helpers
docs.text: Prefer binding only the required local interface. If an owned dependency cannot bind privately, establish and verify narrow confinement before it starts. Check its separately installed service/autostart behavior and keep unrelated firewall rules intact. Restrict Unix sockets to an owned private directory, authenticate peer credentials and define the same-user trust boundary. Use bounded framing, request correlation and partial-write failure handling from the common security chapter. These controls do not turn an unauthenticated API into a remote service.

docs.title: Intentionally remote services
docs.text: Define pairing/authentication, authorization for every action, encrypted transport, credential revocation and the intended exposure. A routing tunnel or address alone is not application authorization. Make remote-control targets and results explicit; never accept arbitrary shell commands as an API. Describe whose infrastructure and continuous connectivity the feature needs before asking users to configure it.

docs.title: Acceptance checks
docs.text:
Test offline/slow/disconnecting peers, malformed/oversized input, invalid credentials, wrong-target replies and expired operations. For IPv4/IPv6 confinement, establish a reachable control on the same path/address family; "unreachable" alone proves nothing about the firewall. Keep isolated namespace tests and physical LAN probes separate. See security and the Mesh example.

Project selector

docs.title: Observation tools and existing-service permissions
docs.text:
An enumerated adapter is not proof that the application acquired a fresh measurement. Preserve interface/permanent source identity, acquisition time, method and original units. NetworkManager AP Strength is percent and LastSeen is CLOCK_BOOTTIME seconds; repeated cached rows do not create new observations. BlueZ cached RSSI is separate from a new RSSI-bearing property event; a metadata update must not silently borrow its old signal. Stop only the discovery session your unique client acquired.

Test the actual launch context. Wireless Surveyor's stationary integration found that direct SSH scan requests were denied on the tested image, while the existing ordinary-user manager/launcher context succeeded under unchanged policy. Report a permission failure precisely; do not infer a missing driver or add privileges from an SSH-only test. This result does not guarantee every image's policy.

A connected test needs its actual local endpoint/interface and association before and after the operation. Bind/attribute DNS separately; an interface-bound TCP socket does not establish where a system-resolver lookup went. Reject late results across pause, capture and source-generation boundaries. Source contract tests can use a private D-Bus and loopback sockets in a network-disabled container, including a real before/after roam and another modeled client's discovery session.

References: NetworkManager AP API, BlueZ Adapter API. These are measurement/ownership contracts, not physical qualification or packet-loss proof.
